Outbound Investment Security Program Regulations

AGENCY: Office of Investment Security, Department of the Treasury.

ACTION: Proposed rule.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: This proposed rule sets forth regulations that would implement 
Subtitle C of the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security 
Act, which is codified at Title VIII of the Defense Production Act. The 
proposed rule would require United States persons to provide 
notification to the U.S. Department of the Treasury regarding certain 
transactions involving foreign persons that are engaged in notifiable 
technologies; and prohibit United States persons from engaging in 
certain other transactions involving foreign persons that are engaged 
in prohibited technologies. Where consistent with Title VIII, the 
proposed rule incorporates certain definitions and concepts from the 
current regulations governing the Outbound Investment Security Program. 
The proposed rule also would add applicability dates to the 
regulations, such that those regulations would continue to apply to 
activities that occurred within the relevant timeframe.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Background

A. Executive Order 14105 and Current Outbound Investment Security 
Program

    On August 9, 2023, Executive Order 14105 (88 FR 54867), 
``Addressing United States Investments in Certain National Security 
Technologies and Products in Countries of Concern'' (the Outbound 
Order), was issued. The Outbound Order described the threat posed to 
the United States by countries of concern that exploit, or have the 
ability to exploit, certain U.S. outbound investments, including 
certain intangible benefits that often accompany U.S. investments and 
that help companies succeed. The Outbound Order identified the People's 
Republic of China (PRC), along with the Special Administrative Regions 
of Hong Kong and Macau, as a country of concern, and identified three 
technology areas for coverage.
    On November 15, 2024, the Department of the Treasury (Treasury 
Department) published regulations to implement the Outbound Order. 
These regulations are found at 31 CFR part 850 (Part 850 Regulations), 
and they established the Outbound Investment Security Program (OISP), 
which went into effect on January 2, 2025. Among other things, the Part 
850 Regulations (1) require U.S. persons to provide notification to the 
Treasury Department regarding certain transactions involving persons of 
a country of concern that are engaged in specified activities in the 
semiconductor and microelectronics and artificial intelligence (AI) 
sectors that may contribute to the threat to the national security of 
the United States; and (2) prohibit U.S. persons from engaging in 
certain other transactions involving persons of a country of concern 
that are engaged in other specified activities in the semiconductor and 
microelectronics, quantum information technologies, and AI systems 
sectors that pose a particularly acute national security threat to the 
United States.
    In the time since the OISP went into effect (approximately 21 
months), the Treasury Department has received approximately 100 
notifications of investments in the semiconductor and AI industries 
from a range of transaction parties, including venture capital firms, 
asset managers, investment banks, and individual investors and 
entrepreneurs. Many other transaction parties and their counsel have 
engaged with the Treasury Department during this time. The Treasury 
Department also has been closely monitoring investment activity that 
may be subject to the OISP, because such investment was either 
potentially prohibited or not notified. Additionally, the Treasury 
Department has engaged with a wide range of stakeholders across 
industries, issued guidance and responses to more than 50 Frequently 
Asked Questions, and launched a website dedicated to the OISP that 
includes an online portal for submission of notifications.

B. Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act of 2025

    On December 18, 2025, Congress enacted the Comprehensive Outbound 
Investment National Security (COINS) Act as part of the National 
Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 (FY26 NDAA). In passing 
the COINS Act, Congress made clear that restricting certain U.S. 
outbound investments into dual-use strategic technologies that benefit 
a foreign adversary's military modernization efforts, surveillance 
states, and human rights abuses is necessary to prevent harm to U.S. 
national security and foreign policy interests. In addition, Congress 
stated that the President should exercise the authorities granted in 
the COINS Act to prevent countries of concern from exploiting U.S. 
capital to undermine U.S. national security and foreign policy 
interests.
    Subtitle C of the COINS Act adds Title VIII to the Defense 
Production Act of 1950, 50 U.S.C. 4581-4589 (Title VIII), and 
establishes a statutory basis for the OISP. In the COINS Act, Congress 
codified the framework for the Secretary of the Treasury (Secretary) to 
(1) require United States persons to provide

[[Page 67397]]

notification to the Treasury Department regarding certain transactions 
involving foreign persons engaged in notifiable technologies, and (2) 
prohibit United States persons from engaging in certain other 
transactions involving foreign persons engaged in prohibited 
technologies. Title VIII maintains various aspects of the current 
OISP--such as its application to certain transactions involving the 
semiconductor and microelectronics, AI systems, and quantum information 
technologies sectors in the PRC including the Hong Kong and Macau 
Special Administrative Regions--while broadening the program to address 
threats to U.S. national security posed by other advanced technologies. 
Specifically, Title VIII expands the OISP's jurisdiction to include two 
new technology sectors (in addition to the three already covered under 
the Part 850 Regulations): (1) high-performance computing and 
supercomputing; and (2) hypersonic systems. Title VIII also authorizes 
the Secretary--in consultation with the appropriate congressional 
committees and subject to notice and comment--to identify additional 
categories of notifiable and prohibited technologies beyond those 
specifically listed in the law that enable the military, intelligence, 
surveillance, or cyber-enabled capabilities of a country of concern, 
and to define the technical parameters of the technologies within those 
categories as reasonably needed for national security purposes.
    Title VIII includes an expanded list of countries of concern. In 
addition to the PRC (including Hong Kong and Macau), Title VIII 
includes as countries of concern the Republic of Cuba, the Islamic 
Republic of Iran, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, the 
Russian Federation, and the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela under the 
regime of Nicol[aacute]s Maduro Moros. Title VIII uses the terms 
notifiable technology and prohibited technology to capture the relevant 
technologies for coverage largely in place of the terms ``notifiable 
transaction'' and ``prohibited transaction'' found in the Part 850 
Regulations. Title VIII uses the term covered national security 
transaction (in place of the term ``covered transaction'' found in the 
Part 850 Regulations) and explicitly excepts from its coverage, among 
other things, underwriting services (including where such services 
involve the acquisition of equity), bank lending, processing or 
clearing of payments, prime brokerage, and global custody services. 
Title VIII also includes exceptions for de minimis transactions, 
specifically for (1) any transaction the value of which the Secretary 
determines is de minimis and (2) certain investments made by a limited 
partner or the equivalent where committed capital is not more than a de 
minimis amount, as determined by the Secretary. Title VIII does not set 
such de minimis values and instead grants the Secretary the discretion 
to do so. Title VIII additionally defines a covered foreign person only 
in terms of such person's relationship to a country of concern and not 
in connection with the technology or technologies in which such person 
engages (in contrast to the Part 850 Regulations, where ``covered 
foreign person'' has a different meaning).
    In addition to certain changes that expand the scope of the OISP, 
Title VIII includes certain new processes. In particular, Title VIII 
requires the Treasury Department to implement regulations establishing 
a process under which a person can request confidential non-binding 
feedback or anonymized public guidance for a potentially prohibited 
transaction. Title VIII also requires the Secretary to establish a 
mechanism for the public to submit evidence on a confidential basis 
with respect to whether a foreign person is a covered foreign person 
engaged in a prohibited technology or a notifiable technology. Title 
VIII further provides the Secretary with the discretionary authority to 
establish a publicly accessible, non-exhaustive database that 
identifies covered foreign persons that are engaged in a prohibited 
technology or a notifiable technology.

II. The Proposed Rule

A. Scope and Structure of the Proposed Rule

    The United States remains committed to maintaining a strong, open 
investment environment and supporting cross-border investment where 
consistent with the protection of U.S. national security. Certain U.S. 
investments, however, may be exploited by countries of concern to 
advance the development of sensitive technologies and products that 
contribute to those countries' military, intelligence, surveillance, or 
cyber-enabled capabilities.
    This current rulemaking seeks comment on the draft regulatory 
framework (Proposed Rule) to implement Subtitle C of the COINS Act. 
Consistent with the sense of Congress, in implementing the COINS Act, 
the Treasury Department seeks to (1) restrict certain U.S. outbound 
investments into certain technologies in countries of concern as is 
necessary to prevent harm to United States national security and 
foreign policy interests; and (2) balance the priority of protecting 
the national security interest of the United States while, to the 
extent practicable, minimizing the cost and complexity of compliance, 
adopting the least burdensome alternative that achieves regulatory 
objectives, and prioritizing transparency and stakeholder involvement 
in the process of issuing the rules.
    To implement Title VIII, Congress has directed the Secretary to 
issue or update current regulations that, as necessary, amend, 
terminate, supersede, revoke, or streamline the existing requirements 
in the Part 850 Regulations. Where consistent with Title VIII, the 
Proposed Rule incorporates certain definitions and concepts from the 
Part 850 Regulations. Where Title VIII uses new or different 
terminology, the Treasury Department has made adjustments while 
seeking, to the extent consistent with congressional intent, to 
preserve relevant aspects of the Part 850 Regulations. This approach is 
intended to minimize the cost and complexity of compliance for affected 
parties by maintaining certain definitions and concepts with which the 
regulated community is already familiar.
    The Proposed Rule, therefore, includes detailed definitions and 
descriptions of terms and elements to clearly delineate the scope of 
coverage and facilitate compliance by U.S. persons. At the same time, 
the Proposed Rule seeks to avoid loopholes that could undermine the 
intent of the COINS Act. The Treasury Department seeks input on how the 
Proposed Rule can best meet these objectives.
    Consistent with Title VIII, the Proposed Rule would place certain 
obligations upon any U.S. person in connection with a covered national 
security transaction in a prohibited technology or in a notifiable 
technology. A covered national security transaction would involve a 
U.S. person's investment in, or other specific activities in connection 
with, a covered foreign person that ``engages in'' a prohibited 
technology or notifiable technology. The proposed definition of covered 
foreign person is based on the person's relationship with a country of 
concern. A covered national security transaction relating to a 
prohibited technology--i.e., where the relevant covered foreign person 
``engages in'' a prohibited technology--would be a prohibited 
transaction, meaning it could not legally be undertaken. As set forth 
in the Proposed Rule, a covered foreign person ``engages in'' a 
prohibited technology when it undertakes an activity specified in the 
definition of

[[Page 67398]]

prohibited technology. The Proposed Rule would define prohibited 
technology to include specific activities in the sensitive technology 
sectors identified in Title VIII or by the Secretary pursuant to 
statutory authority. Meanwhile, a covered national security transaction 
in a notifiable technology--i.e., where the relevant covered foreign 
person ``engages in'' a notifiable technology--would be a notifiable 
transaction, meaning that it would be permitted under the Proposed Rule 
where a U.S. person would need to submit specified information about 
the transaction to the Treasury Department. As set forth in the 
Proposed Rule, a covered foreign person ``engages in'' a notifiable 
technology when it undertakes an activity specified in the definition 
of notifiable technology. The Proposed Rule would define notifiable 
technology to include certain other (i.e., non-prohibited) specific 
activities in the sensitive technology sectors identified in Title VIII 
or by the Secretary pursuant to statutory authority. Further, a U.S. 
person would have certain obligations under the Proposed Rule in 
connection with certain transactions undertaken by any non-U.S. person 
entity that it controls, referred to as a controlled foreign entity. 
These and other terms are defined in Subpart B of the Proposed Rule.
    Under the Proposed Rule, a U.S. person undertaking a transaction 
would have the obligation to determine whether the given transaction is 
prohibited, permissible but subject to notification requirements, or 
not covered by the Proposed Rule because it is an excepted transaction, 
it is exempt, or it is not within the jurisdiction set forth under the 
Proposed Rule. A U.S. person could seek a national interest exemption 
from the prohibition set out in the Proposed Rule by following the 
process described in Sec.  851.502 and further discussed below.
    As directed by Title VIII, the provisions contained in the Proposed 
Rule will not have retroactive effect. The Part 850 Regulations, 
however, will continue to apply to activities occurring between January 
2, 2025, and the effective date of the final regulations implementing 
Title VIII. Nothing in this Proposed Rule limits the authority of the 
Treasury Department or any other department or agency of the U.S. 
Government to take action, including enforcement action, in connection 
with conduct that would be a violation of the Part 850 Regulations, as 
applicable.
    In Section III, the Treasury Department seeks comment from 
stakeholders regarding the provisions of the Proposed Rule. The 
Treasury Department asks commentors to provide, where possible, 
empirical data or other specific information in support of their 
comments.

B. Discussion of the Proposed Rule

    The following discussion provides an overview and narrative 
description of the key substantive provisions of the Proposed Rule to 
implement Title VIII. Because the Part 850 Regulations will remain in 
effect for transactions occurring during the relevant period, the 
Treasury Department views establishing a new Part 851 within Title 31 
of the Code of Federal Regulations with the full process, procedures, 
and requirements under Title VIII as the most administrable approach. 
To make clear the applicability of the Part 850 Regulations, the 
Proposed Rule also would add a new Sec.  850.105 to the Part 850 
Regulations that sets the specific dates for the applicability of those 
regulations.
    Many provisions of the Proposed Rule are substantively identical to 
the corresponding provisions in the Part 850 Regulations. The Proposed 
Rule should be read in its entirety as many terms are related and 
various features are discussed in different parts. The Treasury 
Department will carefully consider all comments provided to the 
Proposed Rule and is particularly interested in receiving comments 
relating to the new provisions and revisions described below.
Subpart A--General
    This subpart includes a general discussion of the Proposed Rule's 
scope, how the Proposed Rule relates to other laws and regulations, the 
similarities and differences between the Proposed Rule and the Part 850 
Regulations, proposed guidance on how to interpret and apply certain 
terms and provisions, the application of the knowledge standard in 
certain circumstances, and, consistent with Title VIII, the role of the 
heads of other relevant Federal departments and agencies in the 
implementation and administration of Title VIII and the Proposed Rule. 
Subpart A of the Proposed Rule would generally be identical in 
substance to Sec. Sec.  850.101 through 850.104 in Subpart A of the 
Part 850 Regulations, with most differences focused on conforming the 
language of the regulatory text to terms used in Title VIII. Proposed 
Sec.  851.101(e) would also revise the Secretary's responsibilities to 
conform to Title VIII's requirements.
    The most significant change in Subpart A compared to the Part 850 
Regulations is an additional element explicitly added to the knowledge 
standard. The Treasury Department proposes to clarify in Sec.  851.104 
that it will take into consideration whether a U.S. person 
appropriately considered any information that the Treasury Department 
has provided to such U.S. person when assessing whether the U.S. person 
conducted a reasonable and diligent inquiry.
Sec.  851.104--Knowledge Standard
    Under the Proposed Rule, certain provisions, including the 
definition of covered national security transaction, would apply only 
if a U.S. person knows of a relevant fact or circumstance. As with the 
Part 850 Regulations, Sec.  851.104 of the Proposed Rule would provide 
explanation and guidance regarding the application of the knowledge 
standard. It would state that if a U.S. person fails to conduct a 
``reasonable and diligent inquiry'' at the time of a transaction and 
undertakes the transaction where a particular fact or circumstance 
indicative of a covered national security transaction is present, the 
Treasury Department may find in the course of determining compliance 
with the Proposed Rule that the U.S. person had reason to know of such 
fact or circumstance (and therefore, for purposes of the Proposed Rule, 
knew). The articulation of the application of the knowledge standard in 
Sec.  851.104 would be similar to that in the Part 850 Regulations. 
This is because Title VIII's definition of knowledge is substantially 
identical to that in the Part 850 Regulations, which indicates 
congressional intent to maintain the Part 850 Regulations' general 
approach to the knowledge standard. Further, consistency in this 
provision minimizes the cost and complexity of compliance for affected 
parties because the regulated community is already familiar with it. As 
such, the Proposed Rule would maintain both the definition of knowledge 
from the Part 850 Regulations (see the discussion of Sec.  851.217 
below), as well as the important explanatory language in Sec.  851.104, 
with certain modifications discussed below.
    The Treasury Department recognizes that for some potential covered 
national security transactions, a U.S. person's ability to conduct 
diligence may be somewhat limited in certain situations, including in 
the context of certain secondary market transactions. The Treasury 
Department reiterates that its assessment of whether a U.S. person has 
undertaken a reasonable and diligent inquiry would under the Proposed 
Rule be based on a consideration of the totality of the relevant facts 
and

[[Page 67399]]

circumstances surrounding the transaction.
    Based on experience operating the OISP, the Treasury Department 
proposes adding at Sec.  851.104(c) of the Proposed Rule an additional 
factor it will consider when assessing whether a U.S. person has 
undertaken a reasonable and diligent inquiry: whether the U.S. person 
appropriately considered information provided by the Treasury 
Department prior to undertaking the transaction, including any 
assessments by the Treasury Department that the relevant covered 
foreign person may be engaged in a notifiable technology or a 
prohibited technology. The Treasury Department would consider the 
provision of such information when determining whether the U.S. person 
had knowledge of certain facts or circumstances. As discussed further 
below, the Treasury Department also proposes adding at Sec.  851.104(e) 
of the Proposed Rule a clarification that the knowledge standard shall 
also apply to the knowledge of a controlled foreign entity for the 
purposes of applying Sec. Sec.  851.402 and 851.403.
Subpart B--Definitions
    The Proposed Rule would preserve several definitions from the Part 
850 Regulations in their entirety; amend certain definitions from the 
Part 850 Regulations; and add several new defined terms both to 
implement the requirements in Title VIII and to make adjustments based 
on feedback received during implementation of the Part 850 Regulations. 
To assist in understanding this Proposed Rule, the discussion below 
notes proposed changes from the Part 850 Regulations and, in certain 
cases, highlights that the Proposed Rule would make no such substantive 
changes.
Sec.  851.202--Affiliate
    The Treasury Department proposes defining the term affiliate to 
mean, in the context of a transaction or activity covered under the 
Proposed Rule, a person that directly, or indirectly through one or 
more intermediaries, controls or is controlled by, or is under common 
control with, a person subject to this part. Under the Proposed Rule, 
if an affiliate of a covered foreign person is included on a list 
enumerated in Sec.  851.226(v), then a covered national security 
transaction involving a covered foreign person engaged in a notifiable 
technology would be a prohibited transaction.
Sec.  851.206--Controlled Foreign Entity
    Title VIII refers to the actions of a controlled foreign entity of 
a U.S. person when explaining the application of the prohibition and 
notification requirement but does not define the term. The Treasury 
Department proposes using the definition of controlled foreign entity 
from the Part 850 Regulations. As noted in the preamble to the Part 850 
Regulations, a controlled foreign entity is an entity incorporated in, 
or otherwise organized under the laws of, a country other than the 
United States of which a U.S. person is a parent. The definition is 
intended to draw a clear line so that it is straightforward for a U.S. 
person to ascertain whether an entity is a controlled foreign entity. 
Of note, Title VIII also uses the term ``controlled foreign person'' in 
reference to the exception for certain intracompany transfers of funds. 
The term ``controlled foreign person'' is not used in the Part 850 
Regulations, and the context for its use in Title VIII is substantially 
similar to that of a controlled foreign entity in the Part 850 
Regulations. Therefore, the Proposed Rule would continue only to refer 
to a controlled foreign entity.
Sec.  851.207--Country of Concern
    Title VIII defines country of concern as the PRC (including the 
Hong Kong and Macau Special Administrative Regions), which is 
consistent with the Part 850 Regulations, and adds Cuba, Iran, North 
Korea, Russia, and the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela under the 
regime of Nicol[aacute]s Maduro Moros. The Proposed Rule would define 
country of concern consistent with the definition in Title VIII.
    With respect to inclusion of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela 
under the regime of Nicol[aacute]s Maduro Moros in Title VIII, that 
regime no longer exists. On March 5, 2026, the United States recognized 
Delcy Rodr[iacute]guez as the head of state of Venezuela and her 
government is not the regime of Nicol[aacute]s Maduro Moros.
Sec.  851.208--Covered Foreign Person
    Title VIII defines a covered foreign person as, subject to 
regulations, a foreign person that (i) is incorporated in, has a 
principal place of business in, or is organized under the laws of a 
country of concern; (ii) is a member of the Central Committee of the 
Chinese Communist Party (CCP) or is a member of the political 
leadership of a country of concern; (iii) is directly or indirectly 
subject to the direction or control of a country of concern, as defined 
by regulation, an entity described in (i) or (ii), or the state or the 
government of a country of concern (including any political 
subdivision, agency, or instrumentality thereof); or (iv) is owned in 
the aggregate, directly or indirectly, 50 percent or more by a country 
of concern, an entity described in (i) or (ii), or the state or the 
government of a country of concern (including any political 
subdivision, agency, or instrumentality thereof).
    Many aspects of the definition of covered foreign person in Title 
VIII generally align with the definition of ``person of a country of 
concern'' in the Part 850 Regulations, and Title VIII provides no 
indication that it was intended to limit the application of the program 
in ways that would permit easy circumvention of its restrictions. The 
Treasury Department therefore proposes defining covered foreign person 
in the Proposed Rule in a manner consistent with the definition of 
``person of a country of concern'' from the Part 850 Regulations. The 
Proposed Rule would maintain the Part 850 Regulations' coverage of 
certain individual foreign persons who are citizens or permanent 
residents of a country of concern. This inclusion is necessary to 
prevent circumvention that would undermine the effectiveness of the 
Proposed Rule. For example, if an individual national of a country of 
concern (who is not a member of the CCP Central Committee or the 
political leadership of a country of concern) chose to redomicile an 
entity that such individual wholly owned to engage in a prohibited 
technology or notifiable technology outside of a country of concern, 
the proposed definition would treat such entity as a covered foreign 
person. Including such individuals also minimizes the cost and 
complexity of compliance for affected parties, in this case by 
maintaining a definition with which the regulated community is already 
familiar.
    Title VIII includes as a category of covered foreign person certain 
foreign persons who are, directly or indirectly, subject to the 
direction or control of a country of concern or certain entities 
associated with a country of concern. For the purpose of the proposed 
definition of a covered foreign person, the Proposed Rule would define 
``subject to the direction or control'' to mean that the government of 
a country of concern (including any political subdivision, political 
party, agency, or instrumentality thereof, or any person acting for or 
on behalf of the government of a country of concern), relevant 
individual, or relevant entity has the power, directly or indirectly, 
to direct or cause the direction of the management or policies of the 
subject entity (whether through the ownership of voting securities, by 
contract, or otherwise).

[[Page 67400]]

    The Proposed Rule would also clarify that the 50 percent aggregate 
ownership requirement in Title VIII can be met through holdings of 
outstanding voting interest, voting power of the board, or equity 
interest. In addition, consistent with the need to prevent 
circumvention and retain features of the Proposed Rule that strengthen 
its effectiveness and are familiar to the regulated community, the 
Proposed Rule would state that this ownership interest also can be held 
by any individual that meets the definition of covered foreign person.
    Additionally, the Treasury Department proposes that where a person 
holds a voting interest, board seat, equity interest, or the 
contractual power to direct or cause the direction of management or 
policies of a covered foreign person, and more than 50 percent of the 
revenue, net income, capital expenditure, or operating expenses of the 
covered foreign person are attributable to that person, then that 
person be considered a covered foreign person. A person would also meet 
this condition if that person holds an interest in more than one 
covered foreign person, and more than 50 percent of the person's 
revenue, net income, capital expenditure, or operating expenses is 
attributable to such covered foreign persons, in aggregate. When 
calculating whether more than 50 percent of the person's revenue, net 
income, capital expenditure, or operating expenses are attributable to 
a given covered foreign person, amounts below $50,000 should not be 
included for purposes of calculating revenue attributable to a covered 
foreign person.
    This provision is intended to align the Proposed Rule's definition 
of covered foreign person with the definition of covered foreign person 
at Sec.  850.209(a)(2) of the Part 850 Regulations. This approach is 
consistent with Title VIII given its coverage of indirect covered 
national security transactions. This approach also addresses potential 
evasion or avoidance pursuant to the Secretary's authority in Title 
VIII, and it furthers the goal of providing clear guidance about 
coverage, while reducing confusion that might be caused by changes from 
the Part 850 Regulations.
Sec.  851.209--Covered National Security Transaction
    Title VIII defines the term covered national security transaction 
as, subject to regulations, a U.S. person's direct or indirect:
    <bullet> Acquisition of an equity interest or contingent equity 
interest in a covered foreign person that the U.S. person knows at the 
time of the acquisition is a covered foreign person;
    <bullet> Provision of a loan or similar debt financing agreement to 
a covered foreign person that the U.S. person knows at the time of the 
provision is a covered foreign person and where the provision affords 
or will afford the U.S. person lender certain financial or governance 
rights characteristic of an equity investment in the covered foreign 
person but not typical of a loan;
    <bullet> Entrance into a joint venture, wherever located, that is 
formed with a person of a country of concern where the U.S. person 
knows at the time of entrance into the joint venture, that the joint 
venture will engage, or plans to engage, in a prohibited technology or 
notifiable technology;
    <bullet> Conversion of contingent equity interest (or equivalent) 
or debt into an equity interest in a covered foreign person;
    <bullet> Acquisition, leasing, or other development of operations, 
land, property, or other assets in a country of concern that will 
result in, or the U.S. person plans to result in, the establishment of 
a covered foreign person or the engagement of a person of a country of 
concern in a prohibited technology or notifiable technology;
    <bullet> Direction of a transaction by a foreign person that the 
U.S. person knows at the time of the transaction would be a covered 
national security transaction if engaged in by a U.S. person, other 
than an acquisition of a limited partner interest or equivalent in a 
non-U.S. person pooled investment fund;
    <bullet> Acquisition of a limited partner or equivalent interest in 
a pooled investment fund where the fund is not a U.S. person and the 
U.S. person knows at the time of the acquisition that such fund likely 
will invest in a person of a country of concern that is in an 
enumerated prohibited technology or a notifiable technology sector, and 
where such fund undertakes a transaction that would be a covered 
national security transaction if engaged in by a U.S. person; and
    <bullet> Any other transaction identified by the Secretary, in 
consultation with the appropriate congressional committees and subject 
to public notice and comment, that is contributing to the military, 
intelligence, surveillance, or cyber-enabled capabilities of a country 
of concern.
    The Treasury Department proposes to implement Title VIII's 
definition of covered national security transaction in a way 
substantively consistent with the statutory text, but with a number of 
important modifications to ensure clarity and consistency with other 
provisions of Title VIII. Specifically, the Title VIII definition of 
covered national security transaction refers in multiple places to a 
``person of a country of concern.'' The term ``person of a country of 
concern'' is not defined in Title VIII but is used in the Part 850 
Regulations. Title VIII also uses the term covered foreign person, 
which appears to be the equivalent of ``person of a country of 
concern.'' As previously discussed, the Proposed Rule would include 
within the definition of covered foreign person some provisions 
currently included in the definition of a person of a country of 
concern in the Part 850 Regulations. Accordingly, the Proposed Rule 
would replace all references to a ``person of a country of concern'' in 
the definition of covered national security transaction with the term 
covered foreign person. Additionally, in each of the relevant 
provisions of the definition of covered national security transaction, 
the Treasury Department proposes to clarify that the relevant knowledge 
that the U.S. person must possess is not merely that the transaction 
involves a covered foreign person, but rather that it involves a 
covered foreign person that engages in a notifiable technology or 
prohibited technology. As reflected in the Proposed Rule, this would 
include specified circumstances in which that engagement is indirect 
because the covered foreign person has one of certain specified 
relationships with a covered foreign person engaged in a notifiable 
technology or prohibited technology. Without this clarification, the 
definition of covered national security transaction would extend to 
transactions without any nexus to relevant technologies.
    In addition, as noted in the discussion regarding the definition of 
covered foreign person, Title VIII and the Proposed Rule do not define 
that term in connection with activity that meets the definition of 
notifiable technology or prohibited technology. A covered national 
security transaction, however, involves a covered foreign person 
engaged in a notifiable technology or prohibited technology. For the 
Proposed Rule to reach a U.S. person investment in a covered foreign 
person or relevant joint venture that meet the conditions set forth in 
Sec.  851.208(a)(8) because of its relationship to one or more covered 
foreign persons that engage in a notifiable technology under Sec.  
851.218(a) through (g) or a prohibited technology under Sec.  
851.226(a) through (u), the Treasury Department would propose to define 
covered national security

[[Page 67401]]

transaction to include where such conditions are met.
    With respect to the provision of a loan or similar debt financing, 
the Treasury Department proposes to incorporate into the definition of 
covered national security transaction clarifications that were included 
in Note 2 to Sec.  850.210 of the Part 850 Regulations.
    The Proposed Rule would make one substantive clarification to the 
definition of covered national security transaction in Title VIII by 
adding a knowledge element to the conversion of a contingent equity 
interest (or equivalent) or debt in a covered foreign person that 
engages in a notifiable technology or prohibited technology or meets 
the conditions of Sec.  851.208(a)(8). This clarification would 
harmonize the conversion prong of the definition of a covered national 
security transaction with the other prongs of the definition and would 
avoid penalizing unwitting activity by a U.S. person that conducted a 
reasonable and diligent inquiry prior to the conversion of such 
interest and lacked reason to know that the contingent equity interest 
was subject to the Proposed Rule. The Proposed Rule would also clarify 
that the conversion prong applies only to a contingent equity interest 
(or equivalent) or debt acquired on or after the effective date that is 
set when the Proposed Rule is finalized.
    The Treasury Department notes that Title VIII incorporates directly 
into the definition of covered national security transaction the 
concept of ``knowingly directing'' present in the Part 850 Regulations 
and, accordingly, extends the scope of ``knowingly directing'' to 
include notifiable transactions. By contrast, the Part 850 Regulations 
limit the application of ``knowingly directing'' to prohibited 
transactions as that term is defined in that part (see 31 CFR 850.303). 
Consistent with Title VIII, proposed Sec.  851.209 incorporates the 
concept of ``knowingly directing'' into the definition of a covered 
national security transaction. Proposed Sec.  851.209(a)(6) also states 
when the Treasury Department considers the criteria in this prong to 
have been met and describes the conditions under which a U.S. person 
may recuse themself from decision-making so as not to be considered 
engaging in such a covered national security transaction. The proposed 
Sec.  851.209(a)(6) closely corresponds to Sec.  850.303 of the Part 
850 Regulations.
    The Treasury Department clarifies that a covered national security 
transaction involving the entrance into a joint venture under Sec.  
851.209(a)(3) would not require the establishment or formation of a new 
entity. The Proposed Rule would not define the term ``joint venture'' 
and instead, the Treasury Department refers to the plain English 
meaning of the term, i.e., as involving the contribution of capital 
and/or assets by two parties and the sharing of profits and losses.
    The Treasury Department also clarifies that U.S. person investments 
in venture capital funds, private equity funds, ``funds of funds,'' or 
other pooled investment funds with pre-existing investments in a 
covered foreign person may constitute an indirect covered national 
security transaction as proposed to be defined in Sec.  851.209(a)(1) 
through (a)(6), separate and apart from whether the acquisition may be 
a covered national security transaction under Sec.  851.209(a)(7).
    The Treasury Department also clarifies that an indirect covered 
national security transaction as proposed could include not only a U.S. 
person's use of an intermediary entity or natural person to engage in a 
transaction that would be a covered national security transaction if 
engaged in directly by a U.S. person, but also a U.S. person's use of a 
transaction structure that obfuscates or conceals the U.S. person's 
role in a transaction that would be a covered national security 
transaction if engaged in directly by a U.S. person.
Sec.  851.210--Develop
    Title VIII does not define develop and the Treasury Department 
proposes to maintain the definition of develop as it exists in the Part 
850 Regulations with three substantive clarifications. First, the 
Proposed Rule would make explicit that the term extends to activities 
engaged in through or in collaboration with affiliates, consistent with 
Title VIII's coverage of indirect covered national security 
transactions. Second, the Proposed Rule would also supplement the list 
of example stages prior to serial production provided in the Part 850 
Regulations by adding the act of transforming blueprints, schema, or 
other plans into a product. Finally, the Proposed Rule would clarify in 
Sec.  851.210(b) that the term develop includes the provision of high-
level oversight, direction, approval, conceptual input, or strategic 
planning in connection with any stage prior to serial production.
Sec.  851.212--Excepted Transaction
    Title VIII identifies certain ``exceptions and clarifications'' to 
the term covered national security transaction but does not use the 
term excepted transaction as that term is used in the Part 850 
Regulations. The Treasury Department proposes to retain the term 
excepted transaction in the Proposed Rule to refer to a transaction 
that is not a covered national security transaction because it meets 
specified conditions. See the discussion in Subpart E below for more 
information.
Sec.  851.214--Foreign Person
    Title VIII introduces the term foreign person but leaves the 
definition to regulations. Accordingly, the Treasury Department 
proposes to define foreign person as any person that is not a U.S. 
citizen or alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence in the 
United States or an entity organized under U.S. law, including any 
foreign branch of such entity, except that for the purposes of Sec.  
851.208(a)(5) through (a)(8), the term foreign person means any person. 
The carveout related to Sec.  851.208(a)(5) through (a)(8) is intended 
to preserve Title VIII's introduction of the term foreign person while 
continuing to capture in the proposed definition of covered foreign 
person those persons that have significant financial or other material 
relationships with covered foreign persons. This approach is consistent 
with the Part 850 Regulations and is intended to prevent circumvention 
of the Proposed Rule and strengthen its effectiveness.
Sec.  851.215--Hypersonic System
    Title VIII adds hypersonic systems as a technology sector in which 
the Secretary may identify prohibited technology or notifiable 
technology. The Treasury Department proposes adding the term hypersonic 
system as a defined term in the Proposed Rule. The term would mean a 
vehicle or weapon delivery system capable of sustained atmospheric 
flight or very low Earth orbit flight at speeds of Mach 5 or greater. 
The Proposed Rule would identify hypersonic glide vehicles, hypersonic 
cruise missiles, hypersonic air-launched or aero-ballistic missiles, 
maneuvering reentry vehicles, and reusable hypersonic vehicles as 
examples of a hypersonic system. Notably, the examples include both 
military and civilian hypersonic systems, which may include systems 
intended for spaceflight. The Treasury Department believes that this 
definition is consistent with industry usage and with other regulatory 
regimes, including export controls, specifically items with Export 
Control Classification Number (ECCN) 9A011 on the Commerce Control List 
and defense articles within Category IV of the United States Munitions 
List.

[[Page 67402]]

Sec.  851.216--Intracompany Transfer of Funds
    Title VIII provides an exception to the definition of covered 
national security transaction for an intracompany transfer of funds 
from a U.S. person ``parent company'' to a ``subsidiary'' located in a 
country of concern, where each of ``parent,'' ``subsidiary,'' and 
``intracompany transfer of funds'' is left undefined. As explained 
above, the Proposed Rule would define a controlled foreign entity to be 
the non-U.S. subsidiary of a U.S. person parent. The Treasury 
Department proposes to define the term intracompany transfer of funds 
to mean the provision of cash or credit by a U.S. person parent to (1) 
support operations of a controlled foreign entity, which operations are 
not in a notifiable technology or a prohibited technology; or (2) 
maintain operations of a controlled foreign entity, which operations 
are in a notifiable technology or prohibited technology that the 
controlled foreign entity was engaged in prior to the effective date 
that is set when the Proposed Rule is finalized at a later time. This 
definition is further discussed below in Subpart E.
Sec.  851.217--Knowledge
    Title VIII defines the terms knowledge and variants such as know as 
they are currently defined in the Part 850 Regulations. The Treasury 
Department proposes to maintain such definition in the Proposed Rule.
Sec.  851.218--Notifiable Technology
    Title VIII introduces the term notifiable technology and, subject 
to regulations, defines it as a technology within the areas of (1) 
semiconductor technology and microelectronics; (2) artificial 
intelligence systems; (3) quantum information technologies; (4) high-
performance computing and supercomputing; or (5) hypersonic systems, in 
each case where not already specified in regulations for prohibited 
technology. This statutory definition makes clear that the Secretary, 
in consultation with appropriate congressional committees and subject 
to notice and comment, may prescribe regulations defining the technical 
parameters of notifiable technologies as reasonably needed for national 
security purposes and may add and define categories to the list of 
technology sectors that enable the military, intelligence, 
surveillance, or cyber-enabled capabilities of a country of concern.
    The Proposed Rule would define certain notifiable technology 
sectors with reference to specific activities and technical parameters 
consistent with the activities and technical parameters in the Part 850 
Regulations, with specific changes and additions that reflect both 
Title VIII's requirement to consider notifiable technology in the areas 
of high-performance computing and supercomputing and hypersonic 
systems, as well as recent advances and developments in the 
semiconductor technology and microelectronics sector, which is 
currently covered by the Part 850 Regulations.
    With respect to changes to the three technology sectors covered by 
the Part 850 Regulations, the most notable involves what was defined as 
AI systems in the Part 850 Regulations and is referred to as ``super 
intelligence systems'' (SI systems) in the Proposed Rule. As discussed 
in more detail below, the Treasury Department, in consultation with 
interagency partners and the Executive Office of the President, has 
determined that the rapid advances in super intelligence capabilities 
of countries of concern warrant a broad prohibition on U.S. person 
investment in that sector. Accordingly, the Proposed Rule lists the 
development of SI systems within the definition of prohibited 
technology, and not within notifiable technology. The Treasury 
Department particularly welcomes comment on this approach, as discussed 
in further detail below.
Semiconductor Technology and Microelectronics
    As with the Part 850 Regulations, the Treasury Department proposes 
including within the definition of notifiable technology the design, 
fabrication, or packaging of any integrated circuit that is not 
included within the definition of prohibited technology (i.e., that 
does not meet the performance parameters and criteria identified in 
Sec.  851.226(c), (d), (e), and (f), as applicable, although these 
criteria differ in certain respects from those in the Part 850 
Regulations). Additionally, the Treasury Department proposes to include 
as notifiable technology the development or production of certain 
equipment not described in Sec.  851.226(b) that is designed or 
intended for use in the design, fabrication, or packaging of any 
integrated circuit. The Proposed Rule would separately define the terms 
fabricate and package, adding further technical detail as to both 
notifiable technology and prohibited technology. The Treasury 
Department assesses that the scope of this notification requirement 
would aid the U.S. Government's visibility into the volume and nature 
of investments of U.S. person transactions involving these technologies 
and products.
SI Systems
    In contrast to the Part 850 Regulations, the Proposed Rule would 
not include development of any SI system within the definition of 
notifiable technology. Instead, the Treasury Department would include 
development of any SI system within the definition of prohibited 
technology, as discussed below.
Quantum Information Technologies
    Similar to the Part 850 Regulations, the Proposed Rule would not 
include any quantum information technologies within the definition of a 
notifiable technology. The Treasury Department would include quantum 
information technologies within the definition of prohibited technology 
as set forth below.
    While Title VIII includes both artificial intelligence systems and 
quantum information technologies in the definition of a notifiable 
technology, Title VIII explicitly states that such technologies are to 
be included in the regulatory definition of a notifiable technology to 
the extent ``not already captured by the technical thresholds 
specified'' in the regulatory definition of a prohibited technology. 
Title VIII also explicitly directs the Secretary, in consultation with 
the appropriate congressional committees and subject to notice and 
comment, to define the parameters of those technologies as reasonably 
needed for national security purposes. For the reasons discussed below, 
the Treasury Department has not proposed any technical parameters 
within which the U.S. Government can permit a covered national security 
transaction into the SI systems or quantum information technologies 
sectors consistent with U.S. national security.
High-Performance Computing and Supercomputing
    The Proposed Rule would include as a notifiable technology the 
development or production of high-bandwidth, low-latency interconnects 
for high-performance computing, including interconnects for system-on-
chip, system-in-package, scale-up networks, and scale-out networks that 
are not otherwise proposed to be prohibited under the Proposed Rule. 
These interconnect technologies and approaches to integration 
contribute to the capability of super intelligence clusters, high-
performance computing environments, and modern data centers through 
high-speed data transfer

[[Page 67403]]

between and effective scaling of compute components.
Hypersonic Systems
    As noted above, the Treasury Department proposes to define 
hypersonic system at Sec.  851.215 as a vehicle or weapon delivery 
system capable of sustained atmospheric or very low Earth orbit flight 
at speeds of Mach 5 or greater, including hypersonic glide vehicles, 
hypersonic cruise missiles, hypersonic air-launched or aero-ballistic 
missiles, maneuvering reentry vehicles, and reusable hypersonic 
vehicles. The Treasury Department would include in the definition of 
notifiable technology the development or production of certain 
technologies capable of use in or for a hypersonic system or its 
components, including sensor, guidance, navigation, or control 
equipment or systems; software for research, modeling and simulation, 
analysis, or testing not included in the definition of prohibited 
technology; and metals, alloys, composites, ceramics, coatings, or 
other materials not included in the definition of prohibited 
technology.
Sec.  851.219--Notifiable Transaction
    Title VIII does not define the term notifiable transaction. The 
Treasury Department proposes using this term to describe the relevant 
language of Title VIII and to promote consistency with the Part 850 
Regulations, in which this term is used, to minimize the cost and 
complexity of compliance for affected parties. Accordingly, the 
Treasury Department proposes to define notifiable transaction as a 
covered national security transaction (that is not a prohibited 
transaction) in which the relevant covered foreign person or relevant 
joint venture (1) engages in a notifiable technology or (2) meets the 
conditions set forth in Sec.  851.208(a)(8) because of its relationship 
to one or more covered foreign persons that engage in a notifiable 
technology.
Sec.  851.221--Parent
    The Proposed Rule would define parent, with respect to an entity, 
as (1) a person that directly or indirectly holds more than 50 percent 
of the outstanding voting interest in an entity or the voting power of 
the board of the entity; (2) the general partner, managing member, or 
equivalent of the entity; or (3) the investment adviser to any entity 
that is a pooled investment fund, with ``investment adviser'' as 
defined in the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 (15 U.S.C. 80b-
2(a)(11)).
    The Treasury Department is considering whether to expand the 
definition of parent to incorporate certain sub-advisers to a non-U.S. 
person fund as well as the general manager (or equivalent) to a non-
U.S. person entity. The Treasury Department welcomes comments on this 
definition.
Sec.  851.222--Party
    Title VIII introduces the term party with respect to a covered 
national security transaction and states that it should have the 
meaning provided in regulations. The Treasury Department proposes 
defining party to mean any U.S. person, any covered foreign person, and 
any foreign person relevant to the covered national security 
transaction, including in the context of joint ventures or controlled 
foreign entities. The term would be used in proposed Sec.  851.902 
concerning submission of information in connection with a request for 
non-binding feedback. The Proposed Rule would require identification of 
``each party to the transaction,'' to include relevant intermediaries, 
financing sources, and controlled foreign entities. Party would also be 
used in Sec.  851.104(c) concerning a U.S. person's reasonable and 
diligent inquiry.
Sec.  851.223--Person
    Title VIII defines person as ``an individual, corporation, 
partnership, association, or any other organized group of persons, or 
legal successor or representative thereof, or any State or local 
government or agency thereof.'' The Treasury Department proposes 
modifying the definition to include any entity--where entity is 
separately defined in the Proposed Rule--rather than listing specific 
types or organizations. The Proposed Rule otherwise would implement 
Title VIII's definition without substantive changes.
Sec.  851.224--Principal Place of Business
    The term principal place of business is used in Title VIII's 
definition of covered foreign person but is not defined, leaving it to 
the Treasury Department to do so in regulations. The Treasury 
Department proposes defining principal place of business in a way that 
is similar to the corresponding definition in the Part 850 Regulations, 
but also specifically includes the location of an entity's headquarters 
and, separately, the location where an entity conducts its main 
business activities. For example, if a company is incorporated and has 
its official headquarters in the United States, but its chief executive 
officer resides and primarily manages the business in a country of 
concern, then the company's principal place of business would be in 
both the United States and the country of concern.
Sec.  851.226--Prohibited Technology
    Title VIII introduces the term prohibited technology, which is 
defined, subject to regulations, as a technology within one of the five 
technology areas enumerated in Title VIII: advanced semiconductor 
technology and microelectronics; artificial intelligence systems; 
quantum information technologies; high-performance computing and 
supercomputing; and hypersonic systems. As with notifiable technology 
discussed above, Title VIII provides the Secretary with the authority, 
in consultation with the appropriate congressional committees, to 
prescribe regulations that define the technical parameters of such 
technology as reasonably needed for national security purposes. The 
Secretary may also add and define technology categories beyond those 
listed in Title VIII that enable the military, intelligence, 
surveillance, or cyber-enabled capabilities of a country of concern. As 
discussed further below, the Secretary, in consultation with 
interagency partners and the Executive Office of the President, has 
determined that the biotechnology sector in countries of concern 
enables the military, intelligence, surveillance, or cyber-enabled 
capabilities of those countries and, therefore, pursuant to his 
authority under Title VIII to prescribe regulations, has added that 
sector to the proposed definition of prohibited technology.
Advanced Semiconductor Technology and Microelectronics
    Consistent with the Part 850 Regulations, the Treasury Department 
proposes including within the definition of prohibited technology the 
development or production of any electronic design automation software 
for the design of integrated circuits or advanced packaging and the 
development or production of any of the following: certain front-end 
semiconductor fabrication equipment designed for performing the volume 
fabrication of integrated circuits (to include extreme ultraviolet and 
deep ultraviolet lithography equipment), equipment for performing 
volume advanced packaging, or other items designed or intended for use 
in or with deep ultraviolet or extreme ultraviolet lithography 
fabrication equipment.
    Further consistent with the Part 850 Regulations, the Proposed Rule 
would also include within the definition of prohibited technology the 
design of any integrated circuit that meets or exceeds

[[Page 67404]]

certain advanced technical thresholds identified by the Department of 
Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), the fabrication of 
certain other advanced integrated circuits that meet certain specified 
parameters, and the development or production of integrated circuits 
manufactured from certain specified semiconductors, certain radiation 
hardened integrated circuits designed to withstand specified high-
radiation environments, and photonic integrated circuits. Additionally, 
the term would include the packaging of any integrated circuit using 
advanced packaging techniques.
    The Proposed Rule also would include within the definition of 
prohibited technology the development or production of high-bandwidth 
memory with a memory bandwidth density greater than 2 gigabytes per 
second per square millimeter. This modification as compared to the Part 
850 Regulations would bring the scope of prohibited technology in this 
sector into alignment with current export control restrictions, 
specifically ECCN 3A090 on the Commerce Control List.
    Also consistent with the Part 850 Regulations, the Proposed Rule 
would separately define the terms advanced packaging, develop, and 
produce, adding further technical detail to the relevant prohibition 
provisions.
SI Systems
    Since publication of the Part 850 Regulations nearly two years ago, 
technology has undergone rapid transformation, with breakthrough 
advances in the capabilities and development of SI systems. A range of 
SI systems developed by covered foreign persons present significant 
national security risks--from the ability to autonomously conduct 
cyberattacks to the potential use by malign actors and foreign 
adversaries to develop weapons of mass destruction. SI systems can also 
provide countries of concern with the potential to substantially 
enhance military modernization efforts, surveillance, and real-time 
targeting and decision-making capabilities. A range of SI systems may 
pose novel national security risks in areas such as cyberattacks and 
the development of chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, or 
explosive weapons, as well as expose novel security vulnerabilities. 
The Treasury Department has observed advances in the capabilities and 
development of SI systems directly through its market monitoring 
activity, receipt of notifications as part of the OISP, and other 
sources.
    The Part 850 Regulations distinguished among ``AI systems'' for 
purposes of the prohibition, the notification requirement, or absence 
from OISP coverage based on the quantity of computing power for 
training, designed end uses, and intended end uses. Over the past two 
years, SI models have achieved notable performance gains through 
additional means other than the quantity of training compute. 
Therefore, no single measure, benchmark, or threshold is currently 
sufficient to distinguish advanced models. Although the quantity of 
training compute may continue to indicate a degree of SI model 
capability, developers increasingly rely on additional methods to 
improve model capability, including other research and development 
activities such as synthetic data generation, improved algorithmic or 
architectural efficiencies, and novel post-training techniques or 
increasing inference-time compute.
    Similarly, the proliferation and adoption of SI capabilities have 
made SI system end uses more challenging to isolate. General-purpose SI 
models that were not necessarily designed to be used for relevant 
national security applications nevertheless may exhibit that 
functionality, and investors may lack insight into the capabilities of 
such models if model developers have not evaluated or advertised these 
capabilities. Additionally, the availability of capable open-source SI 
models that have fewer safeguards and oversight may lead to their 
utilization and incorporation into SI systems in contexts outside their 
intended scope.
    Accordingly, the Secretary, in consultation with interagency 
partners and the Executive Office of the President, has determined that 
it is necessary for national security purposes to define prohibited 
technology to include the development of any SI system. The Treasury 
Department notes that this approach is consistent with the COINS Act's 
direction to balance the priority of protecting the national security 
interest of the United States, while, to the extent practicable, 
minimizing the cost and complexity of compliance for affected parties 
and adopting the least burdensome alternative that achieves regulatory 
objectives. Specifically, this approach seeks to protect U.S. national 
security and streamline compliance through clear proposed regulatory 
text that does not rely on a U.S. person ascertaining the technical 
capabilities or thresholds of SI systems being developed by a covered 
foreign person (which was the case in the Part 850 Regulations).
    Importantly, the Treasury Department proposes to include clarifying 
language regarding when the use or incorporation of certain third-party 
SI systems would or would not constitute the development of an SI 
system. This language generally corresponds to Notes 2 and 3 to Sec.  
850.224 in the Part 850 Regulations.
    The Treasury Department particularly welcomes feedback regarding 
the potential implications arising from defining prohibited technology 
to include the development of any SI system, as well as feedback 
relating to the definition of an SI system. Where possible, feedback 
should discuss impacts, possible alternative approaches aimed at the 
same policy intent described above, and where relevant, should include 
suggestions for how the Proposed Rule could be scoped to address the 
national security concerns described above accounting for the potential 
impact on U.S. businesses and consumers. To the extent that a U.S. 
person believes engaging in a covered national security transaction is 
in the national interest of the United States, the Treasury Department 
notes that the Proposed Rule provides a process by which the U.S. 
person may request an exemption from the Proposed Rule's coverage, 
provided that the Secretary, in coordination with other relevant 
Federal departments and agencies, determines the transaction to be in 
the U.S. national interest. See Subpart E for a further discussion on 
exceptions and exemptions.
Quantum Information Technologies
    The Treasury Department proposes to include within the definition 
of prohibited technology the development of a quantum computer or 
production of any of the critical components required to produce or 
operate a quantum computer (such as a dilution refrigerator or two-
stage pulse tube cryocooler), or the development of software for the 
purpose of designing, simulating, testing, or controlling a quantum 
computer, or for identifying, implementing, costing, or optimizing 
algorithms and applications for a quantum computer.
    The Proposed Rule would also include in the definition of 
prohibited technology the development of algorithms and applications 
for quantum information science technologies. The Proposed Rule would 
include an end-use limitation to appropriately scope this provision to 
refer to activities that could give rise to an acute national security 
threat, recognizing that similar technologies could have important 
civilian purposes.
    The definition of prohibited technology would include the

[[Page 67405]]

development or production of any quantum sensing platform designed for, 
or that the relevant covered foreign person intends to be used for, any 
military, government intelligence, or mass-surveillance end uses.
    The development or production of certain quantum networks and 
quantum communication systems would also be prohibited technology. 
Specifically, prohibited technology would include such networks and 
systems designed for, or that the relevant covered foreign person 
intends to be used for: (1) networking to scale up the capabilities of 
quantum computers; (2) secure communications, such as quantum key 
distribution; or (3) any other application that has any military, 
government intelligence, or mass-surveillance end use.
    The Proposed Rule would separately define the term quantum 
computer, adding further technical detail to the prohibition provision.
High-Performance Computing and Supercomputing
    The Treasury Department proposes maintaining the prohibition in the 
Part 850 Regulations on U.S. person investment with respect to the 
high-performance computing and supercomputing technology area. 
Consistent with the Part 850 Regulations, the definition of prohibited 
technology would include developing, installing, selling, or producing 
any supercomputer enabled by advanced integrated circuits that can 
provide a theoretical compute capacity of 100 or more double-precision 
(64-bit) petaflops or 200 or more single-precision (32-bit) petaflops 
of processing power within a 41,600 cubic foot or smaller envelope, or 
components designed for enabling any of such capabilities of a 
supercomputer. Certain technologies included within the advanced 
semiconductor technology and microelectronics category also are 
relevant to the high-performance computing and supercomputing 
technology area, including the fabrication of any specified DRAM 
integrated circuit, the development and production of any photonic 
integrated circuit (including the development of optical components, 
co-packaged optics, or silicon-photonics integration), and the 
development and production of certain high-bandwidth memory.
Hypersonic Systems
    The Treasury Department proposes to define prohibited technology to 
include the development or production of a hypersonic system, as that 
term is defined in the Proposed Rule (and discussed above), a 
propulsion system capable of enabling hypersonic flight, or fuels or 
propellants for hypersonic propulsion systems. Propulsion systems 
capable of enabling hypersonic flight would include rocket-based 
propulsion, hypersonic airbreathing propulsion such as ramjets and 
scramjets, and combined cycle propulsion.
    The term prohibited technology would also include the development 
or production of certain materials designed for, or that a covered 
foreign person intends to be used for, a hypersonic system, including 
refractory metals or alloys, refractory or ultra-high temperature 
ceramics, certain carbon composites, and stealth coatings, as well as 
the development or operation of specialized infrastructure or a 
facility capable of testing a hypersonic system.
    The Proposed Rule would define prohibited technology to also 
include the development of digital twin technology for modeling and 
simulation of, monitoring, or optimizing a hypersonic system and the 
development of digital thread technology that collects, manages, or 
represents the data flows related to a hypersonic system.
Biotechnology
    Certain advanced or sensitive biotechnologies in countries of 
concern--including those that are subject to export controls, 
biomanufacturing or bioengineering of certain compounds and materials, 
and the technology and equipment capable of being used to engage in 
such manufacturing or engineering--pose an acute risk to U.S. national 
security. Such risks include the proliferation of biological weapons, 
the development of brain-computer interfaces, harm to U.S. supply chain 
security, and the indigenization by countries of concern of advanced 
technologies with military, government intelligence, and mass 
surveillance end uses. U.S. person investments in covered foreign 
persons engaged in such activities are at risk of exploitation. 
Accordingly, pursuant to the authority granted to the Secretary by 
Title VIII, the definition of prohibited technology would include 
specific activities and technical parameters associated with the 
biotechnology sector, as discussed further below.
    Specifically, the Treasury Department proposes to define prohibited 
technology to include the development, engineering, or use of a 
biological system--or component of a biological system--to modify, 
enhance, produce, or control: (1) certain export-controlled agents or 
toxins, as well as novel agents and toxins capable of similar effects 
as those currently export-controlled; (2) energetic precursors or 
energetic materials; (3) novel or high-performance functional materials 
(i.e., bio-derived products that exhibit novel or enhanced properties, 
such as adaptive or protective coatings, materials for agile 
infrastructure, materials capable of self-repair or self-assembly, and 
biosensors); (4) pharmaceutical compounds (e.g., small molecules, 
polymers, vaccines, blood and blood components, allergenics, cell and 
gene therapies, and monoclonal antibodies or other recombinant 
therapeutic proteins), as well as their delivery systems; and (5) 
biofuels (i.e., fuels made or derived from bio-based feedstock). The 
Proposed Rule also would define prohibited technology to include the 
development or production of brain computer interfaces and the 
development, construction, or production of biomanufacturing equipment, 
including components and associated software or technology, as 
identified in ECCNs 2B352, 2D352, and 2E001 on the Commerce Control 
List. The Treasury Department also proposes to include in the 
definition of prohibited technology the development or production of 
certain other related technology or equipment (including components and 
associated software), to include: biological sequencing technology, 
including short-read or long-read sequencing; certain flow cytometers 
and cell sorters; certain liquid chromatography mass spectrometry 
instruments; certain computational or bioinformatics tools; and 
hardware, robotics, or software for automated scientific discovery or 
experimentation, including laboratory automation or cloud lab 
infrastructure.
    It is necessary to place restrictions in this sector in the 
interest of protecting U.S. national security; at the same time, the 
Treasury Department recognizes that restrictions may potentially have 
countervailing effects on national security to the extent restrictions 
lead to significant public health risks or harm U.S. businesses in this 
sector. Accordingly, the Treasury Department is particularly interested 
in comment on this approach. Where possible, feedback should discuss 
impacts, possible alternative approaches aimed at the same policy 
intent described above, and any suggestions for how the Proposed Rule 
could be scoped to address the national security concerns described 
above. In particular, the Treasury Department requests comments on the 
following questions:
    <bullet> Whether or how the Treasury Department should more 
precisely describe the biological systems covered in proposed Sec.  
851.226(r);

    <bullet> Whether the Treasury Department should adjust proposed 
Sec.  851.226(r) to focus on where the development, engineering, or use 
of a biological system is undertaken using equipment identified in 
proposed Sec.  851.226(t) or (u);
    <bullet> Whether or how the Treasury Department should more 
precisely describe the biofuels covered in proposed Sec.  851.226(r), 
such that the Proposed Rule does not include fuels that do not pose

    <bullet> Whether or how a ``novel or high-performance functional 
material'' identified in proposed Sec.  851.226(r)(3) could be more 
precisely described and whether definitions used in other regulatory 
programs, including export controls, could be leveraged to achieve 
additional clarity;
    <bullet> Whether and how ``pharmaceutical compounds'' described in 
proposed Sec.  851.226(r)(4) should be more precisely scoped to focus

    <bullet> Whether the technical parameters of the equipment listed 
in proposed Sec.  851.226(u) should be more precisely scoped to focus 
on advanced or frontier technologies.
    To the extent that a U.S. person believes engaging in a covered 
national security transaction is in the national interest of the United 
States, the Treasury Department notes that the Proposed Rule provides a 
process by which the U.S. person may request an exemption from the 
Proposed Rule's coverage, which could be granted if the Secretary, in 
coordination with other federal departments and agencies, determines 
the transaction to be in the U.S. national interest. See Subpart E for 
a further discussion on exceptions and exemptions.
Cross-Reference to U.S. Government Lists
    The Treasury Department would also include within the definition of 
prohibited technology any notifiable technology engaged in by a covered 
foreign person or relevant joint venture where such covered foreign 
person or joint venture is, or any of its affiliates or subsidiaries 
are, included on one of several U.S. Government lists, such as the 
Entity List maintained by BIS. Defining prohibited technology to 
include notifiable technology engaged in by such persons is reasonably 
needed for national security purposes because the U.S. Government's 
inclusion of such persons on any of these lists reflects a 
determination that the person poses a threat to the foreign policy or 
national security interests of the United States. In addition, defining 
prohibited technology in this manner promotes consistency with the Part 
850 Regulations and provides bright lines for certain U.S. person 
investments, which would minimize the cost and complexity of compliance 
for affected parties while addressing national security risks.
    Section 851.226(v) would cross-reference two additional U.S. 
Government lists beyond those in the Part 850 Regulations: the 
Department of War's list of Chinese military companies under section 
1260H of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021 
and the Office of Management and Budget's list of biotechnology 
companies of concern under the BIOSECURE Act, section 851 of the FY26 
NDAA. Such lists are particularly relevant for the OISP, given their 
focus on entities with connections to the PRC military.
    The Treasury Department also proposes that relevant listed entities 
in Sec.  851.226(v) include the affiliates and subsidiaries of a 
covered foreign person or relevant joint venture that engages in a 
notifiable technology. Prohibiting a U.S. person from engaging in a 
covered national security transaction with a covered foreign person 
engaged in a notifiable technology whose affiliate or subsidiary is 
included on one of the U.S. Government lists would strengthen the 
Proposed Rule by deterring listed persons from establishing 
subsidiaries to engage in a notifiable technology and participate in a 
covered national security transaction that the listed person could not.
Sec.  851.227--Prohibited Transaction
    Title VIII does not use the term prohibited transaction, which was 
used in the Part 850 Regulations. The Treasury Department proposes 
maintaining this term and concept to provide a single term to describe 
the operative language of section 801 of Title VIII and to promote 
consistency with the Part 850 Regulations to minimize the cost and 
complexity of compliance for affected parties. Accordingly, the 
Treasury Department proposes to define prohibited transaction as a 
covered national security transaction in which the relevant covered 
foreign person or relevant joint venture:
    <bullet> Engages in a prohibited technology; or
    <bullet> Meets the investment and financial thresholds under 
proposed Sec.  851.208(a)(8) because of its relationship to one or more 
covered foreign persons that engage in a prohibited technology.
Sec.  851.229--Relevant Federal Departments and Agencies
    The Treasury Department proposes defining the relevant Federal 
departments and agencies as those departments or agencies specifically 
mentioned in Title VIII; i.e., the Departments of State, War, Commerce, 
and Energy, and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence--as 
well as the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative and the Office of 
Science and Technology Policy, and any other department, agency, or 
office the Secretary determines to be appropriate.
Sec.  851.232--Super Intelligence (SI) System
    Title VIII includes ``AI systems'' as a technology area in which 
the Secretary may identify specific notifiable technology or prohibited 
technology. Title VIII does not further define an ``AI system.'' The 
Treasury Department proposes to define super intelligence (SI) system 
\1\ in a manner that is generally consistent with the existing 
definition of an ``AI system'' found in the Part 850 Regulations, but 
with some modifications. The narrative description of the Proposed Rule 
below refers to ``artificial intelligence system'' or ``AI system'' 
when discussing the applicable requirements in the Part 850 Regulations 
or Title VIII and refers to SI system and the abbreviation ``SI'' when 
discussing the Proposed Rule.

    Under Sec.  851.232(a) of the Proposed Rule, an SI system would be
