Subpart C--Prohibited Transactions and Other Prohibited Activities
    Title VIII authorizes the Secretary to prohibit a U.S. person, 
including its controlled foreign entities, from knowingly engaging in a 
covered national security transaction in any prohibited technology. To 
promote consistency with the Part 850 Regulations and to minimize the 
cost and complexity of compliance for affected parties, this subpart of 
the Proposed Rule closely aligns with the text of the Part 850 
Regulations and describes activities that would be prohibited. Such 
activities would include a U.S. person engaging in a prohibited 
transaction unless an exemption has been granted. A U.S. person would 
also be required to take all reasonable steps to prohibit and prevent 
any transaction by its controlled foreign entity that would be a 
prohibited transaction if engaged in by a U.S. person.
Subpart D--Notifiable Transactions and Other Notifiable Activities
    This subpart of the Proposed Rule would require a U.S. person to 
notify the Treasury Department in any of the following circumstances: 
(1) if the U.S. person knowingly undertakes a notifiable transaction; 
(2) if a controlled foreign entity of the U.S. person knowingly 
undertakes a transaction that would be notifiable if undertaken by a 
U.S. person; and (3) if the U.S. person learns following the completion 
date that a transaction that it undertook would have been a covered 
national security transaction if the U.S. person had known of certain 
facts or circumstances at the time of the transaction. In each case, 
the U.S. person would be required to meet certain deadlines and follow 
specified procedures that include requirements to submit detailed 
information to the Treasury Department, certify the completeness and 
accuracy of the information submitted, and maintain records. A U.S. 
person would also be required to promptly notify the Treasury 
Department of any material omission or inaccuracy that the U.S. person 
learns about following any information submission.
    The Treasury Department notes that Sec.  851.402 would clarify that 
a U.S. person must submit a notification when its controlled foreign 
entity undertakes a transaction that the controlled foreign entity or 
the U.S. person knew at the time of the transaction would be a 
notifiable transaction if engaged in by a U.S. person. Section 851.403 
would clarify that a U.S. person's notification obligations in 
connection with post-transaction knowledge apply both to transactions 
undertaken by a U.S. person and to transactions undertaken by a 
controlled foreign entity of a U.S. person. As discussed above, to 
reflect the proposed changes to Sec. Sec.  851.402 and 851.403, the 
Treasury Department proposes to clarify in Sec.  851.104 that the 
knowledge standard would also apply to the knowledge of a controlled 
foreign entity for the purposes of applying Sec. Sec.  851.402 and 
851.403.
    Section 851.405 would expand the information from the Part 850 
Regulations that is required as part of a notification. The items that 
would be added are those that typically have been part of follow-on 
requests for information by the Treasury Department. Including these 
items in the regulatory text is intended to streamline any follow-on 
requests once a notification has been submitted.
Subpart E--Exceptions and Exemptions
    Title VIII gives the Secretary authority to exempt from prohibition 
any activity determined by the President, in consultation with or 
delegated to the Secretary, and in coordination with the Secretary of 
Commerce, Secretary of State, and, as appropriate, the heads of other 
relevant Federal departments and agencies, to be in the national 
interest of the United States. Additionally, Title VIII establishes an 
exemption from prohibition for any authorized intelligence activities 
of the United States.
    This subpart of the Proposed Rule identifies the activities or 
transactions that are not included within the definition of covered 
national security transaction, as discussed below.
Sec.  851.501--Excepted Transaction
    Title VIII identifies, subject to regulations, those transactions 
or activities that are not included within the definition of covered 
national security transaction. Under the Proposed Rule, as in the Part 
850 Regulations, such transactions would be referred to as excepted 
transactions.
    As discussed in more detail below, an excepted transaction in the 
Proposed Rule would include the following (subject to limitations in 
some instances, as explained below):
    <bullet> An investment by a U.S. person in a security that trades 
on a securities exchange or the over-the-counter market in any 
jurisdiction;
    <bullet> An investment by a U.S. person in a security issued by an 
investment company, such as an index fund, mutual fund, or exchange 
traded fund;
    <bullet> An investment by a U.S. person limited partner or 
equivalent in a pooled investment fund as described in Sec.  
851.209(a)(7) where (1) the U.S. person's committed capital does not 
exceed $2 million, or (2) the investment is subject to a specific 
binding contractual assurance regarding a notifiable transaction (for 
purposes of an exception from the notification requirement) or a 
prohibited transaction (for purposes of an exception from the 
prohibition);
    <bullet> An investment in a derivative of any security described 
above;
    <bullet> A U.S. person's full buyout of all equity or interests of 
all covered foreign persons in an entity or assets located outside a 
country of concern;
    <bullet> An intracompany transfer of funds from a U.S. person to 
its controlled foreign entity;
    <bullet> A transaction made after the effective date of the final 
regulations implementing the COINS Act pursuant to a binding, uncalled 
capital commitment entered into before that date;
    <bullet> Acquisition of a voting interest in a covered foreign 
person by a U.S. person lender upon default or other condition of a 
loan made by a lending syndicate;
    <bullet> The receipt of employment compensation by an individual in 
the form of an award of equity or the grant of an option to purchase 
equity in a covered foreign person, or the exercise of such option;
    <bullet> Transactions by a U.S. person that, in the aggregate 
across the preceding 12 months, do not exceed $50,000 in value (for an 
exception from the notification requirement only);
    <bullet> A transaction secondary to a covered national security 
transaction, including certain contractual arrangements or the 
procurement of material inputs for any covered national security 
transaction; bank lending; processing, clearing, or sending of payments 
by a bank; underwriting services; debt rating services; prime 
brokerage; global custody; equity research and analysis; or other 
similar services;
    <bullet> Any ordinary or administrative business transaction;
    <bullet> Any ancillary transaction involving covered foreign 
persons undertaken by a financial institution, such as the processing 
of cash transactions, underwriting and credit rating services, or other 
services ordinarily incidental to the provision of financial services;
    <bullet> Certain transactions that occur in a country or territory 
outside the United States that has been designated by the

[[Page 67408]]

Secretary in accordance with provisions set forth in Sec.  851.501(k) 
of the Proposed Rule; and
    <bullet> Any transactions completed before the enactment of Title 
VIII on December 18, 2025, unless subject to the Part 850 Regulations, 
in which case those rules apply.
    Certain excepted transactions listed above were included in the 
Part 850 Regulations but not specifically included in Title VIII: (1) 
fulfilment of a binding, uncalled capital commitment made prior to the 
effective date of the final regulations; (2) acquisition of a voting 
interest in a covered foreign person upon default or other condition of 
a loan made by a lending syndicate; (3) receipt and exercise of 
employment compensation in the form of equity or options to purchase 
equity in a covered foreign person; and (4) a transaction with or 
involving a country or territory outside the United States designated 
by the Secretary in accordance with criteria that relate to the country 
or territory's own measures to address risks related to outbound 
investment. To further Congress's direction to balance protecting 
national security with minimizing the cost and complexity of compliance 
for affected parties, and to minimize impacts on the smooth functioning 
of U.S. capital markets while still achieving the national security 
objectives of the COINS Act, the Secretary has determined, pursuant to 
the authority provided in Title VIII, that maintaining these excepted 
transactions, with which the regulated public is already familiar, is 
in the national interest of the United States, and therefore includes 
these exceptions in the Proposed Rule. Further explanation regarding 
the Secretary's determination is provided below.
    Fulfilment of a binding, uncalled capital commitment. Including 
this exception in Sec.  851.501 is in the national interest because it 
is intended to avoid disruption to a U.S. person that entered into a 
binding commitment prior to the effective date of the final 
regulations. Such a transaction, however, may be a ``covered 
transaction'' pursuant to the Part 850 Regulations.
    Acquisition of voting interest upon default of a syndicated loan. 
Including this exception is in the national interest because it would 
avoid potential disruption to private credit markets in a narrow set of 
circumstances where a U.S. person lender has passively received an 
interest in a covered foreign person and, even after receiving such 
interest, lacks a role in the lending syndicate that could create the 
opportunity for a U.S. person lender's intangible benefits to transfer 
to the covered foreign person debtor. The Treasury Department welcomes 
comments regarding whether this exception is redundant given Title 
VIII's language regarding the exception for secondary transactions, 
which includes bank lending.
    Receipt of employment compensation in the form of stock or stock 
options and the exercise of such options. Including an exception for 
receipt of employment compensation in the form of equity or the option 
to acquire equity (and the exercise of such an option) in a covered 
foreign person is in the national interest because it avoids 
interference with certain individual U.S. workers' employment prospects 
and potentially personal finances. Moreover, U.S. person employees are 
generally not providing capital to a covered foreign person employer.
    Transactions in certain designated countries or territories. Title 
VIII directs the Secretary, in coordination with the Secretary of 
State, Secretary of Commerce, and the heads of other relevant Federal 
departments and agencies, to engage on both a bilateral and 
multilateral basis with allies and partners to encourage the 
development of mechanisms similar to the OISP to prevent the 
development of prohibited technologies by a country of concern. 
Including an exception for certain transactions occurring in countries 
and territories that develop such similar mechanisms is in the national 
interest because it incentivizes allies and partners to take such 
steps, which helps protect U.S. national security and foreign policy 
interests.
    Details regarding the other exceptions pursuant to Title VIII are 
provided below.
    Publicly traded securities. Title VIII includes as an excepted 
transaction investment in a security, as defined in section 3(a)(10) of 
the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, 15 U.S.C. 78c(a)(10), that trades 
on a securities exchange or the ``over-the-counter'' market in any 
jurisdiction. The Proposed Rule incorporates the exception with minor, 
non-substantive clarifications. The Treasury Department considers this 
exception to be substantively equivalent to the corresponding exception 
in the Part 850 Regulations. As a result, the Treasury Department 
considers that existing guidance available on the OISP website related 
to the publicly traded securities exception would likely be re-issued 
in a manner that applies similarly to this exception under Title VIII.
    Securities issued by an investment company. Title VIII also 
includes an exception for investment in a security issued by an 
investment company, as defined in the Investment Company Act of 1940, 
that is registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission. 
Consistent with Title VIII and with the Part 850 Regulations, the 
Proposed Rule also includes such an exception, along with illustrative 
language from the corresponding exception in the Part 850 Regulations, 
i.e., ``such as an index fund, mutual fund, or exchange traded fund.''
    The Part 850 Regulations also provide for an exception to the 
definition of a covered national security transaction for investment by 
a U.S. person in any company that has elected to be regulated or is 
regulated as a business development company pursuant to section 54 of 
the Investment Company Act of 1940, as amended, at 15 U.S.C. 80a-53. 
Title VIII does not provide for a corresponding exception to the 
definition of covered national security transaction, and the Proposed 
Rule likewise does not include it. The Treasury Department welcomes 
comment on whether extending the exception in Sec.  851.501(a)(1)(ii) 
of the Proposed Rule to an investment in a business development company 
is in the national interest. Title VIII additionally provides the 
Secretary discretion to except investment in a ``security issued by a 
non-United States investment company that is registered with a foreign 
regulator with comparable oversight standards and regulatory 
jurisdiction to the Securities and Exchange Commission as determined by 
the Secretary.'' The Treasury Department does not include this 
exception in the Proposed Rule but invites comment regarding which 
foreign regulators may qualify under Title VIII's standard and the 
potential scope of such an exception.
    Limited partner investments. Title VIII also contains an exception 
from the coverage of limited partner investments when made as a limited 
partner or equivalent in a venture capital fund, private equity fund, 
``fund of funds,'' or pooled investment fund, including where (1) the 
limited partner or equivalent's committed capital is not more than a de 
minimis amount, as determined by the Secretary; and (2) where the 
limited partner or equivalent obtains a binding contractual assurance 
that its capital in the fund will not be used to engage in a 
transaction that would be a covered national security transaction if 
engaged in by a U.S. person. With respect to the first prong, to 
promote consistency with the Part 850 Regulations to minimize the cost 
and complexity of compliance for affected parties, and in light of the

[[Page 67409]]

notifications received to date as part of the OISP, the Secretary has 
determined to set this de minimis value at $2,000,000 in the Proposed 
Rule. With respect to the second prong, the Proposed Rule refers to a 
prohibited transaction or notifiable transaction, as applicable, as the 
corresponding exception in the Part 850 Regulations currently does, 
rather than a covered national security transaction. For clarification, 
the phrase ``as applicable'' means that receipt of a binding 
contractual assurance regarding notifiable transactions would except 
the U.S. person from the notification requirement, while receipt of a 
binding contractual assurance regarding prohibited transactions would 
mean that a U.S. person limited partner or equivalent would not commit 
a violation in the event that the fund used the U.S. person's capital 
to engage in a prohibited transaction, despite such contractual 
assurances. Additionally, the Treasury Department clarifies that this 
exception applies only to limited partner investments covered by Sec.  
851.209(a)(7), consistent with the corresponding exception in the Part 
850 Regulations.
    Derivatives. The Title VIII exception for investments in 
derivatives is explicitly limited to derivatives of a security 
described in three exceptions discussed above: publicly traded 
securities, securities issued by an investment company, and limited 
partner investments. The Proposed Rule maintains this scope for 
exceptions for investments in derivatives although it no longer 
contains the carve-out from the corresponding exception present in the 
Part 850 Regulations for derivatives that confer the right to acquire 
equity, rights associated with equity, or any assets of a covered 
foreign person. The Treasury Department invites comment on whether 
removing this carve-out would create a loophole for U.S. person 
investments that could raise national security concerns.
    Exclusion from exception for investments affording certain 
governance rights. The Secretary also has determined that it is in the 
national interest to exclude from certain exceptions (namely, those for 
investments in publicly traded securities, securities issued by an 
investment company, limited partner investments, and derivatives, each 
as discussed above) covered national security transactions involving 
certain equity investments that would afford the U.S. person certain 
governance rights beyond standard minority shareholder protections with 
respect to a covered foreign person. This carveout would help ensure 
that the exceptions in the Proposed Rule are consistent with the policy 
objectives of Title VIII, and that U.S. persons cannot undertake a 
transaction that has a higher likelihood of advancing the technologies 
that are a core concern of Title VIII. The Treasury Department further 
believes this carveout would be important to protect against potential 
evasion of the Proposed Rule's notification requirements and 
prohibitions. Additionally, the Proposed Rule would include clarifying 
language noting that the relevant ``rights'' of the U.S. person are 
governance-related rights.
    Buyout exception. Title VIII creates an exception similar to the 
buyout exception in the Part 850 Regulations. The Title VIII exception 
appears broader than the exception in the Part 850 Regulations in that 
it applies to a U.S. person's acquisition of all the equity or other 
interests owned or held by a single covered foreign person in an entity 
or assets located outside of a country of concern, while the 
corresponding exception in the Part 850 Regulations requires for its 
application that a U.S. person acquire all equity or interests owned or 
held by all ``persons of a country of concern.''
    The wording of the statutory exception, if left unclarified, could 
introduce administrative challenges for the OISP and create 
interpretive ambiguity. This is so because in the case of an entity or 
assets outside of a country of concern in which multiple covered 
foreign persons hold equity or other interests, excepting a U.S. 
person's buyout of a single covered foreign person's interest in such 
entity or assets could effectively permit U.S. person investment in a 
covered foreign person entity that is engaged in a prohibited 
technology (or allow for such a transaction to go unnotified where the 
covered foreign person is engaged in a notifiable technology) even 
while such covered foreign person continues to have significant, or 
even majority, post-transaction ownership by other covered foreign 
persons. And although Title VIII's language would on its face permit 
such a circumstance, its emphasis on excepting a U.S. person's 
acquisition of the ``totality of the interest'' indicates that Congress 
did not contemplate this scenario. The Proposed Rule, therefore, would 
apply the buyout exception only where a U.S. person acquires all equity 
or interests owned or held by all covered foreign persons such that, 
following the acquisition, the entity no longer constitutes a covered 
foreign person.
    Intracompany transfer exception. Title VIII provides an exception 
for the intracompany transfer of funds, as defined by the Secretary, 
``from a United States parent company to a subsidiary located in a 
country of concern or a transaction that, but for this clause, would be 
a covered national security transaction between a U.S. person and its 
controlled foreign person that supports operations that are not covered 
national security transactions or that maintains covered national 
security transactions that the controlled foreign person was engaged in 
prior to the effective date of the regulations implementing'' Title 
VIII. (Emphases added for clarity.)
    The Proposed Rule would clarify the statutory exception and 
harmonize its terminology with the rest of the Proposed Rule. By 
operation of the proposed definitions of ``parent,'' ``subsidiary,'' 
``controlled foreign entity,'' and ``intracompany transfer of funds'' 
in the Proposed Rule, a U.S. person parent's subsidiary located in a 
country of concern would be a controlled foreign entity, such that the 
relevant exception in the Proposed Rule would refer to the intracompany 
transfer of funds by a U.S. person to a controlled foreign entity. The 
Treasury Department notes that the intracompany transfer exception in 
Title VIII refers to transactions between a U.S. person and its 
``controlled foreign person.'' As discussed above, the term 
``controlled foreign person'' is used only in the intracompany transfer 
exception and does not otherwise appear in Title VIII, and the Proposed 
Rule therefore instead uses the term controlled foreign entity, 
consistent with the other parts of Title VIII and with the Part 850 
Regulations.
    The Title VIII statutory exception also is limited to supporting 
``operations that are not covered national security transactions.'' On 
its face, such language would apply the intracompany transfer exception 
only to investments in entities that themselves engage in covered 
national security transactions. Given the statutory definition's 
similarity to the corresponding exception in Part 850 Regulations, it 
is unlikely Congress intended such a result. To ensure the proper and 
intended operation of Title VIII and to promote consistency with the 
Part 850 Regulations to minimize the cost and complexity of compliance 
for affected parties, the proposed exception (via the definition of an 
intracompany transfer of funds) would refer instead to supporting 
operations that are not in a prohibited technology or a notifiable 
technology.
    The Treasury Department is considering whether and how it should 
further define what it means to

[[Page 67410]] ``maintain operations'' within the intracompany transfer exception. Specifically, the Treasury Department invites comment on whether to (1) adopt a narrow construction of this term, such that the U.S. person parent would be limited to providing capital that would permit the controlled foreign entity to perform no more than upkeep and maintenance of the notifiable technology or prohibited technology; (2) adopt a broader construction to include upgrading or improving the existing operations, but not permitting any expanded production of the technology; or (3) most expansively, adopt a construction that permits expanding production or improving technological capabilities (provided that such improvement does not involve engaging in a different notifiable technology or prohibited technology or shifting from a notifiable technology to a prohibited technology). De minimis transaction. Title VIII also includes an exception for transactions, the value of which the Secretary determines is de minimis. Based on the Treasury Department's experience administering the OISP, the Secretary has determined that the de minimis value should be $50,000, aggregated across the covered national security transactions or provision of funds to the relevant covered foreign person or joint venture in the preceding 12 months. The $50,000 threshold would refer to the value of the transaction or transactions, which can include the provision of funds as well as the fair market value of any non-cash consideration. Pursuant to the authority delegated to the Secretary in Title VIII and as explained in the proposed definition of an excepted transaction, the Treasury Department would not be bound by the U.S. person's determination of the value of a transaction. A U.S. person investor considering the applicability of this exception to a transaction involving non-cash consideration is encouraged to consider valuing such consideration in ways consistent with the equity or other interest acquired in exchange for such non- cash consideration. The Proposed Rule would further limit the application of this exception to transactions that would otherwise be notifiable transactions. A prohibited transaction below this threshold could raise national security concerns given that the technology at issue may enable the military, intelligence, surveillance, or cyber-enabled capabilities of a country of concern. Therefore, the Secretary does not believe that any such transaction should be classified under Title VIII as de minimis. Secondary transaction. Title VIII includes a new category of excepted transaction: a transaction secondary to a covered national security transaction. The Proposed Rule would incorporate the relevant text from Title VIII without modification. The Treasury Department invites comment on the scope of ``contractual arrangements;'' what ``other similar services'' may exist that would constitute a secondary transaction; whether ``bank lending'' would except all ``banks'' from covered national security transactions involving loan provision or similar debt financing; and whether other ``secondary transactions'' are duplicative of any ancillary transactions, including the exception for underwriting services or the processing, clearing, or sending of payments by a bank. Ordinary or administrative business transaction. Title VIII includes an exception for any ordinary or administrative business transaction as may be defined in regulations. The Treasury Department has opted not to include a definition of an ordinary or administrative business transaction in the Proposed Rule. Given the broad scope of the exceptions for ancillary transactions and secondary transactions, the Treasury Department believes that transactions that may fall within the category of ordinary or administrative business transaction likely would already be within the scope of those exceptions or would not be covered national security transactions at all. The Treasury Department welcomes comment on what may constitute an ordinary or administrative business transaction that (1) would meet the definition of a covered national security transaction; and (2) is not otherwise included in another exception in the Proposed Rule. Ancillary transaction. Title VIII creates a new exception for any ancillary transaction undertaken by a financial institution, as ``financial institution'' is defined in 31 U.S.C. 5312. The Proposed Rule would incorporate Title VIII's statutory definition and clarify that such transactions must be undertaken in connection with, or in certain situations, on behalf of, a covered foreign person. Transaction completed before the effective date of Title VIII. Title VIII also includes an exception for any transaction completed before the date of the enactment of Title VIII, i.e., December 18, 2025. The Proposed Rule would implement this provision but limit the application to any covered national security transaction not otherwise subject to the Part 850 Regulations. This additional language is intended to ensure that parties understand that the exception does not permit them to avoid any prohibition or notification requirements under the Part 850 Regulations for any covered national security transaction that would be a ``covered transaction'' under the Part 850 Regulations. Sec. 851.502--National Interest Exemption Title VIII authorizes the Secretary to exempt from prohibition any activity determined by the President, in consultation with the Secretary, or delegated to the Secretary, in coordination with the Secretary of Commerce, Secretary of State, and, as appropriate, the heads of other relevant Federal departments and agencies, to be in the national interest of the United States. Any determination to grant a national interest exemption will be based on a consideration of the totality of the relevant facts and circumstances. Instructions for submitting a request for a national interest exemption can be found on the OISP website. The Treasury Department is considering whether a streamlined process for seeking a national interest exemption would be appropriate for covered national security transactions in one or more technology sectors. The Treasury Department requests comment on what the criteria and timelines should be if any such process were to be considered. Sec. 851.503--Intelligence Activities Exemption Title VIII adds an exemption for any authorized intelligence activities of the United States. Section 851.503 of the Proposed Rule incorporates this exemption. Subpart F--Violations This subpart of the Proposed Rule describes conduct that would be treated as a violation of the Proposed Rule. Such conduct would include taking any action prohibited by the Proposed Rule, failing to take any action required by the Proposed Rule within the timeframe and in the manner required, taking action to evade or avoid--or conspiring to violate--the Proposed Rule's requirements, and making materially false or misleading representations to the Treasury Department when submitting any information required by the Proposed Rule. The Treasury Department notes that the proposed anti-evasion language would apply to any action that evades or avoids, has the purpose of evading or avoiding, causes a violation of, or attempts to violate any of the Proposed [[Page 67411]] Rule's obligations, as well as to any conspiracies formed to violate the obligations of the Proposed Rule. Evasion may include the establishment by a U.S. person of an entity or corporate structure to effectuate a transaction that would be a covered national security transaction if undertaken by a U.S. person. While many U.S. investors or asset managers may have bona fide commercial reasons to establish non-U.S. investment vehicles to effectuate investments outside of the United States, in determining whether an entity was established or used for the purpose of evading the obligations of the Proposed Rule, the Treasury Department may consider, inter alia: whether a U.S. person de facto controls the non-U.S. entity irrespective of formal corporate governance rights or voting interest held in the entity; the extent and nature of any shared personnel, services, facilities, or branding between a U.S. person and the non-U.S. entity, or commingling of funds; privity in limited partnership interest between a U.S. person and the non-U.S. entity (i.e., does the non-U.S. entity have the same investors as an affiliated U.S. fund or fund controlled by a U.S. person); and shared beneficial ownership or right to proceeds (including any commercial arrangements effectuating the same) between the U.S. person and the non-U.S. entity. Pursuant to Title VIII, the Treasury Department proposes adding a new Sec. 851.605, which would establish that, in an enforcement action for a violation of the Proposed Rule, the burden of proof shall be upon the Secretary. Subpart G--Penalties and Disclosures This subpart of the Proposed Rule describes the penalties that would be applicable to violations of the Proposed Rule. The Treasury Department notes that the current Part 850 Regulations contain text that allows for civil and criminal penalties. Title VIII, however, includes language regarding civil penalties but does not include language regarding criminal penalties. As such, the Treasury Department proposes to retain previous civil penalty language from the Part 850 Regulations in the Proposed Rule and to omit language that allows for criminal penalties from the Proposed Rule. The Proposed Rule would include civil penalties up to the maximum amount set forth in section 206 of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, 50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq. The Treasury Department may impose a civil penalty on any person that violates the Proposed Rule. Further, to implement Title VIII, the Proposed Rule would also state that the Secretary may compel the divestment of a covered national security transaction in a prohibited technology. This subpart would also describe the process for submission of a voluntary self-disclosure by a person that may have violated applicable rules. The Treasury Department may take self-disclosures into account as a mitigating factor in determining any appropriate response, including the potential imposition of penalties, if the Treasury Department determines that there was a violation. Consistent with Title VIII, the Proposed Rule would use corresponding language from the Part 850 Regulations but would modify the scope of a voluntary self- disclosure to require that such disclosures contain a proposal for mitigation of any harms associated with the violation, including divestment or a voluntary disgorgement of profits. The Proposed Rule would further specify the information that must be included in a voluntary self-disclosure letter. Subpart H--Provision and Handling of Information This subpart of the Proposed Rule would implement the section of Title VIII that provides that information or documentary material provided to the Treasury Department under this part is exempt from disclosure under section 552(b)(3) of Title 5 of the United States Code. Title VIII also identifies exceptions to this rule. The Proposed Rule would incorporate this provision of Title VIII with certain clarifications. Title VIII excepts from the disclosure exemption certain information ``[g]athered by the Secretary or the Secretary's designee where the disclosure is determined to be in the national interest.'' Section 851.801(b)(6) would clarify that the determination is made by the Secretary or the Secretary's designee. Factors that the Secretary or the Secretary's designee may consider when determining if disclosure is in the national interest may include whether such disclosure will further national security interests, address law enforcement needs, or promote compliance with the rule. Circumstances in which the Secretary may determine the disclosure of information to be in the national interest can include, for example, in the context of notifying the public regarding an action taken by the Treasury Department to enforce compliance with the Proposed Rule. The Treasury Department anticipates this exception to be invoked only in circumstances in which the Secretary identifies a national interest that disclosure could help to address. Subpart I--Non-Binding Feedback This subpart would implement Title VIII by establishing procedures by which an eligible person may request non-binding feedback from the Treasury Department regarding a prohibited transaction. The Treasury Department recognizes that parties may have questions regarding whether a specific investment would constitute a prohibited transaction. Indeed, since the Part 850 Regulations became effective in January 2025, transaction parties and the public have requested feedback on interpretations of the Part 850 Regulations, submitted questions regarding compliance with the regulations, and sought additional public guidance. In response, the Treasury Department has published on its website several tranches of Frequently Asked Questions designed to assist the public with understanding and complying with the regulations. To make effective and efficient use of the Treasury Department's resources, limit frivolous requests as contemplated under Title VIII, and adhere to Title VIII's confidentiality requirements, the Proposed Rule would require that requests for feedback be submitted in writing by a party with a direct financial interest in an actual--not hypothetical--transaction. IV. Rulemaking Requirements

    This Proposed Rule is intended to implement Subtitle C of the COINS 
Act, which added Title VIII to the Defense Production Act of 1950. 
Title VIII establishes a statutory framework for the Secretary to (1) 
require U.S. persons to provide notification to the Treasury Department 
regarding certain transactions involving foreign persons that are 
engaged in activities involving notifiable technologies, and (2) 
prohibit U.S. persons from engaging in certain other transactions 
involving foreign persons that are engaged in activities involving 
prohibited technologies.
    The Treasury Department has opted, as a matter of discretion, to 
undertake a high-level analysis of the anticipated costs and benefits 
of the Proposed Rule.
    In addition, this section includes the required assessments of the 
reporting and recordkeeping burdens under the Paperwork Reduction Act 
of 1995 (PRA), 44 U.S.C. 3501 et seq., and the potential impact on 
small entities pursuant to the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA), 5 
U.S.C. 601 et seq.

A. Executive Orders 12866 and 13563

    Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 direct agencies to assess costs 
and benefits of available regulatory alternatives for certain types of 
rulemaking in certain circumstances and, if regulation is necessary, to 
select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits. The Office of 
Management and Budget's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs 
has designated this Proposed Rule a significant regulatory action under 
E.O. 12866. The Treasury Department conducted an assessment of the 
costs and benefits of the Proposed Rule, as well as the costs and 
benefits of available regulatory alternatives.
    As noted above, Title VIII directs the Secretary to issue 
regulations to (1) require U.S. persons to provide

[[Page 67413]]

notification to the Treasury Department regarding certain transactions 
involving foreign persons that are engaged in activities involving 
notifiable technologies, and (2) prohibit U.S. persons from engaging in 
certain other transactions involving foreign persons that are engaged 
in activities involving prohibited technologies. The Proposed Rule 
maintains the general framework of the Part 850 Regulations while 
making changes to implement Title VIII and address the effort by 
countries of concern to develop certain technologies that pose a threat 
to the national security of the United States.
    Title VIII authorizes the Secretary, in consultation with the 
appropriate congressional committees and subject to notice and comment, 
to prescribe regulations defining the technical parameters of 
notifiable technologies and prohibited technologies in the following 
technology sectors: (1) semiconductor technology and microelectronics; 
(2) artificial intelligence systems; (3) quantum information 
technologies; (4) high-performance computing and supercomputing; and 
(5) hypersonic systems. As described above, the Treasury Department has 
determined that rapid advances in the development, adoption, and use of 
SI capabilities by countries of concern warrant an expansion in the 
prohibition of U.S. person investment in that sector. Additionally, for 
the reasons described above, the Treasury Department has expanded the 
prohibition on U.S. person investment into semiconductors and quantum 
computing in countries of concern. Title VIII also authorizes the 
Secretary, in consultation with the appropriate congressional 
committees, to add and define categories of technologies and products 
that enable the military, intelligence, surveillance, or cyber-enabled 
capabilities of a country of concern. The Secretary has determined for 
purposes of this Proposed Rule to add certain technologies and products 
within the biotechnology sector as prohibited technologies. Other 
changes include the coverage of additional countries of concern: 
Russia, Iran, Cuba, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, and 
Venezuela under the regime of Nicol[aacute]s Maduro Moros. Title VIII 
also requires that the implementing regulations establish a process 
under which a person can request confidential non-binding feedback or 
anonymized public guidance for a potentially prohibited transaction.
    The Proposed Rule would apply to certain types of investments by 
U.S. persons in covered foreign persons engaged in the technologies and 
activities described above or meets the conditions of Sec.  
851.208(a)(8). These include certain acquisitions of equity interests, 
limited partner investments, greenfield investments, joint ventures, 
and certain debt financing transactions. The Proposed Rule would except 
from coverage certain activities or transactions that are identified in 
Title VIII, including investments in publicly traded securities, 
certain investment funds, any de minimis transaction, any ancillary 
transaction, an intracompany transfer of funds, or any ordinary or 
administrative business transaction, as well as other transactions

authorizes the Secretary to except from coverage any other transaction 
that the Secretary determines is in the national interest of the United 
States.

B. Costs

    The primary direct costs to the public associated with the Proposed 
Rule would relate to (1) understanding the Proposed Rule, (2) 
conducting the transaction-specific diligence that would be needed for 
a U.S. person to determine whether its intended transaction would be 
subject to either the notification or prohibition provisions of the 
Proposed Rule; and (3) if applicable, preparing and submitting a 
mandatory notification of certain transactions or other information to 
the Treasury Department pursuant the Proposed Rule. The Treasury 
Department requests comments on any of the assumptions and estimates in 
this analysis.
    The Proposed Rule would apply to all U.S. persons undertaking a 
covered national security transaction with or involving a covered 
foreign person. To estimate the number of potential transactions 
subject to the Proposed Rule, the Treasury Department considered the 
number of transactions filed under the notification requirement 
pursuant to the Part 850 Regulations, the scoping of the Proposed Rule, 
and a review of commercially available data on transactions that may be 
subject to the Proposed Rule based on the identified sector of the 
investment target.
    For example, to estimate the number of entities and transactions 
that would be potentially affected by the Proposed Rule and would incur 
associated compliance costs, the Treasury Department considered 
publicly available data from PitchBook relating to transactions from 
approximately 2023 through 2025. This data indicated that over the 
relevant three-year period, almost 230 unique U.S.-based investors 
completed approximately 300 initial and add-on investment transactions 
in the semiconductor, artificial intelligence, quantum information 
technology, hypersonic system, high-performance computing and 
supercomputing, and biotechnology sectors (as such sectors are 
identified in the commercially available data) in countries of concern. 
This data suggests an annual average of 75 different investors 
collectively engaging in an annual average of approximately 100 
potentially covered national security transactions. While granular 
details of U.S. private investment overseas cannot be determined with 
precision, the Treasury Department believes this figure to be a 
reasonable estimate. For purpose of this analysis, the Treasury 
Department then doubled the averages from this data over the relevant 
three-year period to account for the possibility that these average 
figures undercount transactions. For example, commercially available 
data may not include certain transactions that would be subject to the 
Proposed Rule, or such data may not identify certain transactions as 
occurring in the technology sectors subject to the Proposed Rule. Thus, 
the Treasury Department's analysis is based on the assumption that, 
annually, around 150 different investors collectively engage in 200 
transactions that would be potentially covered by the Proposed Rule.
    The Treasury Department is interested in comments regarding 
additional publicly available data sources that the Treasury Department 
should consider. The Treasury Department also welcomes comment on 
whether doubling the averages from publicly available data is a 
reasonable way to account for uncertainty or whether the Treasury 
Department should account for this uncertainty using a different 
methodology.

The Proposed Rule also contemplates that a person seeking a national interest exemption from the prohibition requirements of the Proposed Rule would submit certain information to the Treasury Department. For purposes of this analysis, however, the Treasury Department has assumed that U.S. persons will perform due diligence with respect to 200 potentially covered national security transactions each year, and that all 200 transactions are notifiable transactions. The Treasury Department has made this assumption in the interest of estimating an upper bound. As a general matter, a notifiable transaction would likely cost more in terms of time and resources than a prohibited transaction, because, in addition to the due diligence cost, a notifiable transaction would entail extra time to prepare and submit a notification. However, the Treasury Department expects that some prospective transactions subjected to due diligence would turn out to be not covered and others would turn out to be prohibited; transactions that are not covered national security transactions and prohibited transactions would not trigger a notification. If a respondent submits information in support of a national interest exemption, the Treasury Department anticipates that the associated time needed to prepare and submit such information would be comparable to the costs of preparing and submitting a notification. The Treasury Department anticipates that the time and cost of preparing and submitting a post-transaction notice, notice of any material omission or inaccuracy in any previous representation, statement, or certification, or responding to agency inquiries may be comparable but likely lower than the costs of preparing and submitting a notification. Additionally, the Treasury Department recognizes that a U.S. person may incur costs for the preparation of a request for confidential non- binding feedback or anonymized public guidance. However, since this is an optional request for a U.S. person and is a new addition to the existing program, the Treasury Department cannot estimate the number of requests that may be submitted. Therefore, the Treasury Department has determined that costs associated with the non-binding feedback process will not be included in this cost estimate. Additional Indirect Costs Associated With Prohibited Transactions With respect to prohibited transactions, the Treasury Department does not believe that the Proposed Rule will have additional direct economic costs to U.S. investors beyond those described above. There may, however, be additional indirect costs associated with prohibited transactions. Investors who would have otherwise engaged in a prohibited transaction, absent the Proposed Rule, may have to seek less promising investment opportunities since they would be precluded from undertaking and benefiting from prohibited transactions that would be foreclosed to them by the Proposed Rule. These indirect costs amount to the difference between the return that would have been generated by the prohibited transaction and the return that would result from the best alternative transaction. In addition, while the Proposed Rule may have an economic impact on investment targets that are covered foreign persons because certain transactions would be prohibited, the Proposed Rule is not designed to, nor does it, prohibit all U.S. person investments into such persons, due to the several exceptions provided for in the Proposed Rule. Benefits As Congress noted in the COINS Act, there are countless known and unknown entities in countries of concern that are developing dual-use strategic technologies that benefit a foreign adversary's military modernization efforts, surveillance states, and human rights abuses. Advancement by countries of concern in sensitive technologies and products critical for the military, intelligence, surveillance, human rights abuse, or cyber-enabled capabilities of such countries constitutes a threat to the national security of the United States. Restricting certain U.S. outbound investments into certain technologies in countries of concern is necessary to prevent harm to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. The Proposed Rule is designed to complement existing tools of the U.S. Government and effectively address the threat to the national security of the United States described in Title VIII. While the benefit of protecting national security is difficult to quantify, the Treasury Department has identified specific benefits below. The notification function of the Proposed Rule is intended to provide key information that the Treasury Department could use to better inform the development and implementation of the OISP. Such notifications received under the existing OISP have increased the U.S. Government's visibility into transactions by U.S. persons, or their controlled foreign entities, in the SI and the semiconductor and microelectronics sectors in a country of concern. These have also assisted the U.S. Government by highlighting trends with respect to related capital flows and investment by non-U.S. persons in these technology sectors in a country of concern. Finally, these notifications have informed policy development for the Proposed Rule as well as other U.S. Government efforts to protect U.S. national security. The Treasury Department expects to receive similar benefits from notifications filed under the Proposed Rule. The Treasury Department does not currently propose a breakeven analysis for the Proposed Rule, as it continues to collect information on potential costs and benefits of the Proposed Rule through the rulemaking process. D. Alternatives The Proposed Rule is promulgated pursuant to Title VIII, which directs the Treasury Department to issue regulations to implement its requirements. However, the Treasury Department considered some alternative approaches that would be consistent with Title VIII. Specifically, the Treasury Department considered the following potential alternatives to the Proposed Rule: Limited exceptions. In the Proposed Rule, the Treasury Department would define the term ``covered national security transaction'' largely as defined in Title VIII (as set forth in Subpart B) without further permitted additions and would provide for certain exceptions (in Subpart E), some of which are explicitly required by Title VIII and others that are permitted, but not required, under Title VIII. Therefore, as an alternative consistent with Title VIII, the Treasury Department could have proposed a broader definition of covered national security transaction and/or fewer exceptions. This alternative likely would result in the gathering of more information on U.S. investments in sensitive technologies and products in countries of concern through notifiable transactions, which would expand the information available to assist the development and implementation of the OISP. But the alternative approach also likely would impose higher compliance costs on U.S. persons. Prohibited and notifiable technology using broad definition of sectors rather than specific activities and technologies. In the Proposed Rule, the Treasury Department would define notifiable technology and prohibited technology in Sec. 851.218 and Sec. 851.226, respectively, by reference to certain technologies and activities, and in some instance, end uses. Alternatively, and consistent with Title VIII, the Treasury Department could have proposed broad sectoral categorizations, such as, for example, defining a prohibited technology to include ``all super intelligence'' in a country of concern. If the Treasury Department had proposed that approach, the Treasury Department estimates that it would create ambiguity and uncertainty for U.S. persons about what investments were subject to the prohibition and notification requirements because of the lack of a clear, articulated nexus between a covered foreign person and the technology being described. This in turn would result in significant compliance costs and overall economic consequences on U.S. persons and the U.S. economy that could undermine potential national security benefits. The Proposed Rule would also require any U.S. person that files a notification to maintain a copy of the notification filed and supporting documentation for a period of ten years from the date of the filing. Regulatory Flexibility Act It is hereby certified that the Proposed Rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities within the meaning of section 601(6) of the Regulatory Flexibility Act. The Proposed Rule may impact any U.S. person, including a small business that engages in a covered national security transaction with a covered foreign person. The Treasury Department does not anticipate that the Proposed Rule would affect ``small organizations'' or ``small governmental jurisdiction[s],'' as defined in the RFA. The Treasury Department expects the Proposed Rule to have a negligible baseline impact on small businesses because the Proposed Rule focuses on certain transactions that--based on the Treasury Department's experience with the type of U.S. investors involved in transactions currently subject to the existing OISP--are more likely to involve a small number of sophisticated investors managing substantial amounts of capital and with access to expertise in a number of emerging technology sectors. This expertise may be acquired through affiliated companies or the hiring of senior advisors with significant experience growing and managing successful technology companies, either of which financial investors that meet the requirements to be a small business are unlikely to have. Further, the covered foreign persons subject to the Proposed Rule are largely located outside of the United States, requiring U.S. investors to hire or retain staff skilled in assessing and structuring complex cross-border investments in foreign companies, which is not common to small businesses. In addition, and as discussed below, the Treasury Department has assessed that small businesses would be more likely to enter into the types of transactions excepted from coverage, including de minimis transactions and investments in publicly traded securities, if such businesses are investing at all into covered national security transactions. As an example, the Small Business Administration's (SBA's) Table of Size Standards with respect to North American Industry Classification System U.S. Industry Sector 52 ``Finance and Insurance'' defines a small business in this sector by dollar value rather than by number of employees. For example, SBA categories such as ``open end investment funds,'' and ``other financial vehicles'' are not considered small businesses if their average annual receipts exceed $40 million. A number of the U.S. investors who have submitted notifications pursuant to the Part 850 Regulations are investment firms or entities that exceed this threshold, as do most investment entities operating in the United States. As a reference point, according to the Investment Company Institute, there were 11,263 U.S. businesses in this [[Page 67418]] category with net sales of $1.58 trillion.\4\ Extrapolating from this data, the average net sales per firm in this category would have been $140.4 million. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- \4\ Investment Company Institute, 2026, Investment Company Factbook, Data Tables https://www.icifactbook.org/26-fb-data-tables.html#sec9. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- Given the applications of technologies and products in these sectors, the Treasury Department believes investments into these sectors involving a person of a country of concern is not typical for a small business, as these investor types are treated in the SBA's Table of Size Standards. Importantly, the Proposed Rule would also except certain types of transactions, including certain investments into publicly traded securities or into certain investment funds, as well as de minimis transactions where a small business is more likely to consider investing. Given the narrow scoping of what constitutes a covered national security transaction under the Proposed Rule, the Treasury Department expects that few small businesses, as that term is defined by SBA, will be impacted by the Proposed Rule. In the unlikely event that a small entity is subject to the requirements of the Proposed Rule, such entity would be expected to incur the costs described in the separate cost benefit analysis above. For submission of notifications, the Treasury Department has endeavored to develop information gathering procedures that minimize the burden on U.S. persons, both large and small. U.S. persons who file a notification will use a fillable form that will be available online and is intended to facilitate submission through an electronic format. This fillable form will benefit anyone who submits a notification, regardless of their size, but may be especially helpful for small businesses that will be able to submit directly to the Treasury Department through the online portal. Notwithstanding this certification, the Treasury Department invites comments from the public about the impact the Proposed Rule would have on small entities. Authority: 50 U.S.C. 4581-4589; 31 U.S.C. 321. Subpart A--General Sec. 851.101 Scope. (a) This part implements Title VIII of the Defense Production Act of 1950, as amended (50 U.S.C. 4581-4589) (Title VIII), which directs the Secretary of the Treasury (the Secretary), in consultation with the Secretary of Commerce, the Secretary of State, and, as appropriate, the heads of other relevant Federal departments and agencies (as defined in Sec. 851.229), to issue, subject to public notice and comment, regulations to require a U.S. person to provide written notification on behalf of itself or its controlled foreign entity regarding certain covered national security transactions in any notifiable technology and, where the Secretary has exercised the authority under Title VIII to prohibit certain transactions, to prohibit a U.S. person and its controlled foreign entities from engaging in certain covered national security transactions in any prohibited technology. (b) This part identifies certain types of transactions that are covered national security transactions--which are certain transactions by a U.S. person into or with a covered foreign person. Additionally, this part identifies other instances where a U.S. person has obligations with respect to certain transactions. The regulations prescribe exceptions to the definition of covered national security transaction. A transaction that meets an exception is not a covered national security transaction and is referred to as an excepted transaction. Finally, this part: (1) Exempts any authorized intelligence activities of the United States; and (2) Prescribes a process to consider exempting certain activities from the definition of a covered national security transaction on a case-by-case basis. (c) This part identifies categories of covered national security transactions that are notifiable transactions. A notifiable transaction is a covered national security transaction by a U.S. person or its controlled foreign entity with a covered foreign person or a relevant joint venture involving a notifiable technology. A notifiable transaction includes a U.S. person's direction of a transaction that the U.S. person knows would be a notifiable transaction if engaged in by a U.S. person (other than an acquisition of a limited partner interest or equivalent in a pooled investment fund that is not a U.S. person). This part requires a U.S. person to notify the Department of the Treasury of each such notifiable transaction by such U.S. person or its controlled foreign entity. This part also requires a U.S. person to provide prompt notice to the Department of the Treasury upon acquiring actual knowledge after the completion date of a transaction of facts or circumstances that would have caused the transaction to be a covered national security transaction if the U.S. person had such knowledge on the completion date. Additionally, any person who makes a representation, statement, or certification to the Department of the Treasury under this part is required to promptly notify the Department of the Treasury upon learning of a material omission or inaccuracy in such representation, statement, or certification. (d) This part identifies categories of covered national security transactions that are prohibited transactions. A prohibited transaction is a covered national security transaction by a U.S. person with a covered foreign person or relevant joint venture involving a prohibited technology. This part prohibits a U.S. person from knowingly engaging in a prohibited transaction, which includes a prohibition on a U.S. person's direction of a transaction that the U.S. person knows would be a prohibited transaction if engaged in by a U.S. person (other than an acquisition of a limited partner interest or equivalent in a pooled investment fund that is not a U.S. person). This part also requires a U.S. person to take all reasonable steps to prohibit and prevent any transaction by its controlled foreign entity that would be a prohibited transaction if undertaken by a U.S. person. (e) This part provides for the imposition of civil penalties for any violation, and the Secretary has the authority to compel divestment of a covered national security transaction in a prohibited technology. Pursuant to Title VIII, the Secretary also is required to establish a process to identify covered national security transactions for which no notification was submitted and for which information is reasonably available. (f) The Secretary should, as appropriate: (1) Coordinate with the Secretary of Commerce, the Secretary of State, and the heads of other relevant Federal departments and agencies, to determine whether certain activity is in the national interest of the United States and should be exempted from prohibition; (2) Consult with the Secretary of Commerce, the Secretary of State, and,

Sec.  851.104  Knowledge standard.

    (a) Certain provisions of this part apply only if a U.S. person 
knows of a fact or circumstance. The term knowledge is defined in Sec.  
851.217. In determining whether a U.S. person is complying with this 
part or has violated any obligation under this part, the Department of 
the Treasury will assess whether such person has or had knowledge of 
the relevant facts and circumstances at the specified time.
    (b) Such assessment as to whether, at the time of a given 
transaction, a U.S. person has or had knowledge of a given fact or 
circumstance will be made based on information a U.S. person had or 
could have had through a reasonable and diligent inquiry. A U.S. person 
that has failed to conduct a reasonable and diligent inquiry by the 
time of a given transaction may be assessed to have had reason to know 
of a given fact or circumstance, including facts or circumstances that 
would cause the transaction to be a covered national security 
transaction in a notifiable technology or a prohibited technology.
    (c) In assessing whether a U.S. person has undertaken such a 
reasonable and diligent inquiry, the Department of the Treasury's 
considerations will include the following, as applicable, among others 
that the Department of the Treasury deems relevant, with respect to a 
particular transaction:
    (1) The inquiry a U.S. person has made regarding an investment 
target or other relevant party, including questions asked of the 
investment target or relevant party, as of the time of the transaction;
    (2) The contractual representations or warranties the U.S. person 
has obtained or attempted to obtain from the investment target or other 
relevant party with respect to the determination of a transaction's 
status as a covered national security transaction in a notifiable 
technology or a prohibited technology and the status of an investment 
target or other relevant party as a covered foreign person;
    (3) The efforts by the U.S. person as of the time of the 
transaction to obtain and consider available non-public information 
relevant to the determination of a transaction's status as a covered 
national security transaction in a notifiable technology or prohibited 
technology and the status of an investment target or other relevant 
party as a covered foreign person;
    (4) Available public information, the efforts undertaken by the 
U.S. person to obtain and consider such information, and the degree to 
which other information available to the U.S. person as of the time of 
the transaction is consistent or inconsistent with such publicly 
available information;
    (5) Whether the U.S. person purposefully avoided learning or 
seeking relevant information;
    (6) The presence or absence of warning signs, which may include 
evasive responses or non-responses from an investment target or other 
relevant party to questions or a refusal to provide information, 
contractual representations, or warranties;
    (7) The use of available public and commercial databases to 
identify and verify relevant information of an investment target or 
other relevant party; and
    (8) Whether the U.S. person appropriately considered any 
information made available by the Department of the Treasury prior to 
the completion of the transaction, including any assessments by the 
Department of the Treasury that the relevant covered foreign person may 
be engaged in a notifiable technology or a prohibited technology.
    (d) An assessment of whether a U.S. person has undertaken a 
reasonable and diligent inquiry shall be based on a consideration of 
the totality of relevant facts and circumstances.
    (e) Paragraphs (a) through (d) of this section shall also apply to 
the knowledge of a controlled foreign entity for the purposes of
